text: Construct the application so that shared clients, pools, and other process-scoped resources are initialized in the FastAPI/Starlette lifespan and closed during lifespan teardown. Avoid network calls, client creation, migrations, or expensive initialization as accidental module-import side effects. An application factory is optional, but must be used if multiple differently configured app instances, test isolation, or deferred construction requires it.

Parse production configuration through typed settings and reject missing, empty, malformed, internally inconsistent, or development-only values before the process becomes ready. Validate origins and URLs structurally, numeric ranges explicitly, and booleans without ambiguous ad hoc string coercion. Do not log secret values.

Fail startup when an internal component required to serve any meaningful request cannot initialize. Treat third-party availability as a readiness or degraded-service decision unless that provider is indispensable to every request. Required database connectivity may affect readiness; optional payment, email, image, or messaging providers should not automatically create fleet-wide restart loops.

On termination, stop accepting new traffic, allow a bounded period for in-flight requests and background tasks to finish, then close resources. Configure the hosting platform’s termination grace period to exceed or align with Uvicorn’s graceful-shutdown timeout.

Do not use development reload mode in production. Run Uvicorn under a hosting platform, container orchestrator, or process supervisor that restarts failed processes and supports graceful termination. An additional standalone process manager is not mandatory when the platform already provides equivalent supervision.

Choose worker and instance count from measured CPU, memory, latency, connection, and workload behavior. Ensure every worker performs its own lifespan initialization and receives consistent configuration. Prefer one process per container where the orchestrator scales containers; multiple workers in one host are valid when the host does not provide equivalent process-level scaling.

Set and document Uvicorn keep-alive, concurrency limit, maximum-request recycling if used, and graceful-shutdown timeout. Treat Uvicorn’s concurrency limit as an overload backstop, not a replacement for endpoint-aware rate limiting. Disable or minimize server-identification headers where supported and verify actual edge responses.

Trust `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Proto`, or related forwarding metadata only when the immediate network peer is a known proxy address or network. Configure the allowlist from the actual deployment path. Never accept forwarding headers directly from arbitrary public clients, and use `*` only when network isolation guarantees that every direct peer is a sanitizing proxy.
classification: REQUIRED when forwarded headers are consumed

text: Define how multiple proxy hops are normalized and which component appends, replaces, or strips forwarding fields. Verify original scheme, host, client IP, path prefix, generated absolute URLs, redirects, and OpenAPI server URLs. Configure ASGI `root_path` or equivalent when the API is mounted below an external prefix.
classification: REQUIRED when deployed behind one or more proxies

text: Enforce an explicit production host allowlist at the edge or with Starlette `TrustedHostMiddleware`; include only canonical API domains and deliberate aliases. Handle preview deployments through controlled patterns or separate environment configuration, not an unrestricted wildcard.
classification: STRONGLY RECOMMENDED; REQUIRED if request host influences URL generation, routing, cookies, redirects, or security decisions

text: Serve the public API only over HTTPS. Terminate TLS at a managed edge or load balancer unless end-to-end TLS is required by the network model. Redirect HTTP to HTTPS at one authoritative layer. Application-level HTTPS redirects are appropriate only when the application receives a trustworthy original-scheme signal; otherwise they can loop behind TLS termination. Enable HSTS only after the selected host and any included subdomains are consistently HTTPS-capable.
classification: REQUIRED for HTTPS; STRONGLY RECOMMENDED for HSTS after safe rollout

text: When browser and API origins differ, allow only exact, reviewed frontend origins; explicitly allow required methods and request headers, including `Authorization` and `Content-Type`; expose only response headers the frontend needs, such as a request ID. Do not accept `null` origins unless a documented client requires them. Dynamic matching must validate against a closed rule and must never reflect an arbitrary origin.
classification: REQUIRED for cross-origin browser access; NOT APPLICABLE for same-origin-only deployments

text: Do not set `allow_credentials=True` merely because JavaScript manually sends a bearer token. It is required when cross-origin Fetch uses credentials mode `include`—for example, browser-managed cookies, HTTP authentication, or client certificates. Regardless of credentials mode, `Authorization` must be explicitly allowed because it is a CORS non-wildcard request-header name.

Establish an explicit security-header policy, with browser-document headers primarily attached to React HTML and interactive API documentation rather than indiscriminately to JSON. At minimum, verify HSTS at the HTTPS edge, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, cache directives, and removal or minimization of server-identification headers.

Apply finite request-body, multipart, individual-part, file, field-count, header, URL/query-string, and decoded-content limits before expensive parsing or storage. Use edge/proxy limits for coarse rejection and application/parser limits for endpoint-specific enforcement. Reject oversized content with `413`; use `431` where supported for excessive request headers.

Select limits from legitimate use, maximum expected image and JSON sizes, parser memory, downstream provider limits, instance capacity, and abuse cost. Do not adopt one universal numeric limit. Document whether limits apply to compressed bytes, decompressed bytes, each multipart part, aggregate content, and chunked transfers.

Bound collection page size, cursor/offset range, search term length and complexity, sort/filter combinations, date ranges, export size, and bulk-operation item counts. Reject or clamp excessive values consistently and document defaults and maximums.
classification: REQUIRED for collection, search, export, and bulk endpoints

text: Define a layered timeout budget for connection establishment, request headers, request body, application processing, database work, and each upstream provider. Configure slow-client/header/body protection at the proxy or hosting edge; Uvicorn keep-alive alone is not a complete slowloris defense. Ensure downstream timeouts are shorter than the caller’s remaining budget.

Treat application request cancellation as a normal condition. Ensure cancellation closes response streams and releases database/provider resources. Do not continue irreversible work after client disconnect unless the operation has been deliberately transferred to durable background processing. Use `202 Accepted` only when work has genuinely been accepted but is not complete, with a way to observe outcome where appropriate.

Apply endpoint-specific abuse controls based on identity and cost: IP or network for unauthenticated traffic; user/token for authenticated traffic; and tighter controls for public search, messaging, content creation, upload initiation, payment initiation, administrative mutations, and authentication-related endpoints. Combine burst and sustained policies where needed.
classification: REQUIRED for abuse-sensitive and resource-expensive flows

text: In multi-instance deployments, use a limiter architecture that provides the intended consistency scope. Local per-worker counters may be acceptable only when limits are explicitly approximate. Define limiter failure behavior by endpoint: fail-open can preserve availability for low-risk reads; fail-closed may be justified for costly or high-abuse mutations but creates a limiter-driven denial-of-service risk. Return `429` and an appropriate `Retry-After` when a retry interval is known.

Return a stable JSON error contract with an HTTP status, machine-readable type or code, safe human-readable message, and request/correlation ID. RFC 9457 Problem Details is a suitable standard form but is not mandatory if an equally stable documented schema is used.

Install global handlers for request validation, malformed JSON, application exceptions, provider failures, and unexpected exceptions. Never return stack traces, SQL/provider messages, raw exception strings, secret values, or internal filesystem/module details. Log the internal exception separately with the request ID. Ensure debug mode is disabled in production.

Distinguish malformed syntax (`400`), syntactically valid but invalid input (`422` where that contract is chosen), unsupported media type (`415`), oversized content (`413`), state conflicts or duplicates (`409`), missing/precondition failures (`404`/`410`/`412`), and transient server or gateway failures (`500`/`502`/`503`/`504`). Conceal resource existence with `404` instead of `403` only where the authorization policy requires it.

Permit only documented HTTP methods. Preserve safe and idempotent semantics: do not make `GET` mutate state; design `PUT` and `DELETE` so repetition has the intended idempotent effect; do not assume `POST` is idempotent without an application-level mechanism. Return `405` with `Allow` for known routes that reject a method.

Require `Content-Type: application/json` for JSON request bodies and reject unsupported media types with `415`. Honor or explicitly constrain `Accept`; return JSON consistently and consider `406` when the client excludes every supported representation. Multipart upload endpoints must declare and enforce their multipart contract separately.

Serialize JSON as UTF-8; use RFC 3339 timestamps with an explicit UTC `Z` or numeric offset; define UUIDs as canonical strings; and document nullability. Do not transmit money through binary floating-point where exact decimal semantics matter—use integer minor units or a documented decimal-string representation. Define unknown-field handling explicitly.
classification: STRONGLY RECOMMENDED; exact money representation is CONTEXT-DEPENDENT

text: Define response models for every non-streaming JSON endpoint and use them to validate and filter output. Separate input, internal persistence, public response, administrative response, and provider schemas. Reject or deliberately ignore unexpected input fields according to endpoint risk; sensitive mutations should normally reject unknown fields.
classification: REQUIRED for endpoints returning sensitive or user-derived data

text: Bound large responses. Use pagination for collections, avoid unbounded in-memory serialization, and use streaming only where the client and proxy timeout/caching behavior is deliberately designed. Enable compression only above a useful minimum size and test latency and memory effects; do not rely on compression as a substitute for response limits.

Generate or validate a bounded, syntactically safe request ID for every request, return it in the response, and include it in access and application logs. Treat arbitrary client-supplied IDs as untrusted: reject, replace, or normalize malformed and excessive values. Propagate a correlation identifier to downstream calls and durable background work. Full distributed tracing is optional.

When W3C Trace Context is adopted, parse `traceparent` according to the specification, ignore invalid values, create a new context as required, and avoid placing personal or secret information in `traceparent` or `tracestate`. Do not let a caller force expensive sampling.

Emit structured access logs containing, as operationally justified, timestamp, method, route template rather than raw sensitive path, status, duration, request ID, trusted client IP, safe pseudonymous user identifier, response size, error category, authentication outcome, and rate-limit outcome. Keep access, application, security, and audit events logically distinct.

Never log bearer tokens, `Authorization`, cookies, passwords, API or webhook secrets, presigned URLs, full payment data, sensitive request bodies, private-message content, or unnecessary personal data. Sanitize CR/LF and other control characters in untrusted values. Restrict audit events to necessary identifiers and changes, not secret payloads.

Set an explicit cache policy for every response class. Prevent shared-cache reuse of user-specific, administrative, inbox, notification, payment, or private-message responses through `private`, `no-store`, appropriate `Vary`, or another demonstrably safe policy. Do not assume that authentication alone always prevents caching, and do not assume every authenticated response requires `no-store`.

Use validators such as ETags and conditional requests for cacheable public resources where beneficial. Ensure cache keys vary on every representation-selecting input, including relevant query parameters, `Origin` when CORS output varies, and any negotiated representation. Never place secrets, bearer tokens, or presigned URLs in cache keys that are exposed through dashboards or logs.

Provide separate liveness and readiness semantics when the hosting platform uses probes. Liveness should answer whether the process/event loop is functioning and should not fail merely because a third party is down. Readiness should answer whether the instance should receive normal traffic, using short, bounded checks only for dependencies necessary to serve that traffic.
classification: REQUIRED when platform routing depends on probes; otherwise STRONGLY RECOMMENDED

text: Keep health responses minimal, uncached, and free of secrets, stack traces, connection strings, environment dumps, hostnames, or dependency versions. Protect detailed diagnostics by network restriction or authentication; keep orchestrator probes reachable through their trusted path. Exempt probes from ordinary user quotas only through a non-spoofable source or dedicated internal route.

Expose a non-sensitive build/release identifier where operationally useful, but do not publish secret environment configuration or detailed component versions. A version endpoint is not a substitute for an endpoint inventory or software inventory.

Decide deliberately whether Swagger UI, ReDoc, and OpenAPI JSON are public, authenticated/internal, or disabled. Do not treat hiding documentation as an authorization control. If exposed, ensure schemas omit secrets and internal-only fields, declare bearer security schemes, document error responses and limits, and carry accurate API/release metadata.

Maintain backward compatibility for deployed clients or coordinate breaking changes atomically. Treat removal or renaming of fields, new required request fields, narrowed enums, changed field types, altered status codes, changed error codes/shapes, and endpoint removal as potentially breaking. Added response fields and enum values can also break strict or exhaustively coded clients and therefore require contract testing.

Mark deprecated operations and fields in OpenAPI and use the `Deprecation` response header where machine-readable runtime notice is useful. Use `Sunset` only when a retirement time is planned, and communicate migration guidance through documentation or a link. Do not remove an endpoint merely because it was marked deprecated.

Use URL, header, or media-type versioning only when independent client lifecycles or long-lived incompatible contracts justify it. Operating without an explicit version is acceptable when frontend and backend deployment is tightly coordinated and changes remain compatible.

Maintain an authoritative inventory of public, authenticated, administrative, health, webhook, documentation, and legacy endpoints, including every deployed hostname and preview environment. Remove or protect obsolete routes and ensure alternate/beta hosts receive the same critical limits and headers.

Apply stricter, endpoint-specific controls to messaging, user-content creation, upload initiation/completion, payment initiation, and administrative mutations. Webhooks normally do not require CORS because they are server-to-server, but still require HTTPS, strict media/body limits, timeouts, replay/idempotency policy where applicable, and abuse protection that does not block legitimate provider retries.
classification: REQUIRED for exposed high-cost or sensitive workflows

text: Keep HTTP parsers, proxy software, and Uvicorn current; reject ambiguous HTTP/1.1 message framing; ensure the edge and origin agree on `Content-Length` and transfer-coding behavior; and prevent clients from bypassing the canonical proxy to reach an inconsistently parsing origin.

Complete an end-to-end production verification suite against the real deployed edge, not only an in-process test client. Include positive, negative, abuse, timeout, cache, proxy-spoofing, shutdown, and documentation-exposure scenarios, and retain sanitized evidence.

Every protected backend request must verify the presented Firebase **ID token** with the maintained Firebase Admin SDK for the explicitly configured production project. A custom token, refresh token, arbitrary JWT, or merely decoded JWT must not be accepted as an application bearer credential.

Successful verification must establish that the signature is valid, the signing key is trusted, `aud` matches the intended Firebase project ID, `iss` is the corresponding Secure Token issuer, the token is not expired, `iat` is acceptable, `sub` is nonempty and represents the Firebase UID, and the configured clock-skew allowance is no greater than the documented SDK limit.

The backend must fail closed for missing credentials, empty tokens, malformed JWTs, invalid signatures, unsupported algorithms, wrong projects, expired tokens, malformed `Bearer` syntax, or ambiguous/multiple authorization credentials. It must not select one of multiple conflicting credentials.

ID tokens must be transmitted only over validated HTTPS and in the HTTP `Authorization: Bearer <token>` field. Tokens must not be accepted from URLs, query strings, route parameters, fragments, referrers, or ordinary form fields.

Application, proxy, tracing, analytics, error, and crash-reporting systems must redact the `Authorization` value and must not persist raw ID tokens, refresh tokens, custom tokens, or App Check tokens. Browser code must not print them to the console.

The browser must use Firebase SDK APIs such as `getIdToken()` and auth/token-change observers rather than directly reading, persisting, copying, or refreshing raw token material. The application must not introduce a second custom `localStorage` or `sessionStorage` token copy.

Firebase persistence mode must be an explicit risk decision. Administrator sessions should use session-only or otherwise restricted persistence on shared or unmanaged devices; ordinary-user persistence may be longer where the product accepts the XSS/device-loss tradeoff.

Request retry logic must obtain a current token after an authentication-expiry response and retry an idempotent request at most under a bounded policy. It must not blindly replay non-idempotent mutations, create infinite refresh loops, or fan out simultaneous refreshes unnecessarily.

Client sign-out must clear the local Firebase session and application caches, but security-sensitive “sign out all devices” or compromise actions must additionally revoke Firebase refresh tokens. The system must not treat client `signOut()` as global token revocation.

The application must define a revocation policy. At minimum, revocation-aware verification or an equivalent current-user check must be used for suspended/disabled accounts, administrator access, account security changes, and other high-risk operations. Checking revocation on every protected request is acceptable but incurs an additional remote lookup; selective checking is acceptable only when local account-state enforcement prevents revoked privileges from remaining usable.
classification: `REQUIRED` for high-risk and lifecycle events; otherwise `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`

text: Password change, primary-email change, suspected compromise, user-requested global sign-out, administrator suspension, and emergency privilege removal must trigger the documented invalidation sequence: update the authoritative local state where applicable, revoke Firebase refresh tokens, and force clients to refresh or sign out.

A disabled Firebase user must be rejected by protected endpoints through `check_revoked=True` or a current Firebase-user lookup where that check is required. Local suspension must still be enforced independently. Re-enabling Firebase must not automatically reactivate a locally suspended user.

Authentication failures caused by invalid credentials must return a safe `401` challenge without exposing token contents or detailed cryptographic diagnostics. Temporary Firebase certificate/API failures must fail closed, use bounded retries where the SDK supports them, and return a temporary service failure rather than treating the request as authenticated.

The application must not cache a positive authentication result beyond the verified token’s expiry, and must not use cached authentication to bypass current local account-state or administrator-role checks. Raw token strings must not be cache keys visible in telemetry.

Tokens should not be forwarded to downstream services unless that service is an intended trusted verifier for the same Firebase project and needs the end-user identity. Prefer forwarding a derived, minimal internal identity context over the original bearer token.

Email verification must be enforced according to operation risk, not universally by assumption. Public browsing may remain open; hosting, messaging, payment-related actions, account recovery, or abuse-prone features may require verified email. Administrator access must require a verified and currently controlled identifier. Verification status must be taken from a current token/user record, not indefinitely cached.

Recent authentication or step-up authentication must be required for password changes, primary-email changes, account deletion, provider linking/unlinking, MFA enrollment/removal, recovery-factor changes, data export, and similarly sensitive account operations. Payment-method metadata changes and sensitive profile changes require a documented risk decision.
classification: `REQUIRED` for Firebase-designated sensitive account operations; otherwise `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`

text: Password reset, sign-in, registration and account-recovery responses must resist account enumeration through generic client messages and materially similar response behavior. Email enumeration protection must remain enabled unless an approved exception documents the resulting exposure. Rate limits and abuse controls must cover sign-in, registration, reset, verification resend and recovery attempts.

Recovery links and codes must be verified through Firebase, restricted to authorized continuation domains, used over HTTPS, and not exposed in analytics or logs. Custom handlers must validate the action code and operation before applying it. Support personnel must not bypass identity proofing by directly changing credentials solely on the basis of easily obtained profile data.

Firebase password-policy configuration must be inspected and intentionally selected. The application must not rely on composition rules alone; it should permit long passwords, avoid forced periodic changes absent compromise, and combine provider controls with rate limiting and MFA according to risk.

Firebase MFA for ordinary player accounts may be optional or risk-triggered. Administrator accounts must use MFA. TOTP is preferable to SMS where Firebase-native factors are used; phishing-resistant authentication through a suitable identity provider should be preferred for the highest-risk administrators where feasible.

App Check may be used as an additional signal for the custom FastAPI backend by requiring and verifying App Check tokens in a dedicated header. It must not replace Firebase user authentication, local authorization, rate limiting, anti-automation controls, or transaction safeguards.
classification: `STRONGLY RECOMMENDED` for exposed abuse-prone browser APIs; otherwise `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`

text: App Check limited-use/replay-consumption mode should be reserved for low-volume, high-value operations where its extra remote call, quota and latency are justified. Debug tokens must never be shipped or committed and must be deleted when exposed.

PostgreSQL must be the authoritative source for application roles, administrator status, account state, ownership, hosting eligibility and dynamic permissions. Firebase custom claims may be a derived cache or frontend/security-rule hint, but must not be an independent conflicting authority for backend authorization.

Only trusted backend code and tightly controlled operators may set custom claims. Claims must contain no secrets or mutable profile data, must remain below Firebase’s serialized 1,000-character limit, and must avoid reserved claims. A role reduction must update PostgreSQL first and must not wait for claim propagation to remove backend access.

The Firebase Admin SDK must use an attached managed identity with Application Default Credentials on Google Cloud, or Workload Identity Federation/another short-lived identity mechanism off Google Cloud, whenever supported. Long-lived service-account JSON keys are a fallback, not the preferred production design.

Firebase Admin credentials must never enter frontend bundles, public environment variables, source control, container layers, build artifacts, logs or crash reports. An unavoidable JSON key must be stored in a secret manager or protected file mount with minimal filesystem access and a documented rotation/revocation process.

The backend service account must be single-purpose and granted only the Firebase Authentication permissions it actually needs. Broad project Owner, Editor, Firebase Admin, or unrestricted service-account impersonation must not be used where narrower roles or custom roles suffice.

User-managed service-account key creation and upload should be disabled by organization policy where no justified key use exists. Any remaining keys must be inventoried, attributed, rotated, tested for disablement, and removed when unused. Emergency revocation must account for already issued short-lived access tokens.
classification: `STRONGLY RECOMMENDED`; key inventory `REQUIRED` if keys exist

text: Development, automated testing, staging and production must use isolated Firebase projects and credentials. Each frontend and backend environment must use the matching project configuration, and wrong-environment tokens must fail audience/project verification. The Auth Emulator may be used for tests but not production.

Every local user must have an immutable association to the Firebase UID, protected by a non-null unique constraint. A separate local primary key may be used for business relationships. Email must not be the identity-join key.

First-login or registration provisioning must be idempotent and safe under concurrent requests. It must use the UID uniqueness constraint and transactionally return the one resulting local account rather than creating duplicate rows or partially initialized users.

Provisioning before successful Firebase authentication must not create an active application account solely from untrusted client identity fields. If preregistration records exist, they must be inert and bound to the authenticated UID through a controlled claim process.

Firebase is authoritative for Firebase UID, sign-in providers, verified-email state and provider-managed contact attributes. PostgreSQL is authoritative for application display/profile data where the user can edit it, roles, account status, hosting eligibility, ownership and permissions. Every copied Firebase attribute must have a documented refresh rule.

Email comparisons used for display, notification or lookup may be normalized consistently, but normalization must not merge two local accounts or transfer authorization. An old email reused by a new Firebase UID must create or map to a distinct local identity unless an explicit, authenticated account-linking procedure proves ownership of both accounts.

Provider linking and account merging must require a currently authenticated user, recent authentication where sensitive, conflict detection, and an explicit policy for reconciling two existing local accounts. Automatic merging solely because emails match is prohibited.

Every authenticated request must resolve the current local user by Firebase UID and enforce the current local account state. A token for a nonexistent, suspended, deleted, or otherwise disallowed local account must not gain normal protected access.

Account states must have an explicit access matrix. `active` ordinarily permits policy-controlled access; `suspended` and `deleted` deny normal actions; `pending deletion` may permit only cancellation, status, export or support functions selected by policy; narrower restrictions such as “hosting disabled” must be enforced only on affected functions.
classification: `REQUIRED` for an explicit matrix; individual limited-access choices `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`

text: Local suspension must take effect before or atomically with any external Firebase action. The local status must block new protected operations immediately; refresh-token revocation and Firebase disablement should be added where a full authentication stop is intended. Partial Firebase failure must not reactivate application access and must enter a retry/reconciliation state.

Suspension workflows must be idempotent and concurrency-safe, must record the current state and authorized reason, and must define restoration behavior. Restoration may re-enable Firebase only when local policy allows it and must not silently restore prior administrator privileges or bypass current restrictions.

Account deletion must require recent authentication for self-service requests and must first enter an application-controlled non-active state before destructive external work. Existing sessions must lose normal access promptly through local-state enforcement and Firebase revocation/disablement or deletion.

Immediate deletion, delayed deletion, soft deletion and anonymization are policy alternatives. If a cancellation period is chosen, the pending user may receive only explicitly allowed functions and cancellation must reauthenticate the user and verify that irreversible work has not already begun. No retention period should be inferred from Firebase documentation.

Deletion must be an idempotent, resumable workflow that tracks completion of Firebase deletion/revocation, local anonymization or deletion, notification cleanup, content handling, and external-provider actions. Retries must distinguish “already deleted” from failure. Reconciliation tooling must expose incomplete steps without exposing secrets.

Deletion must classify dependent data rather than blindly cascade everything. Authentication/profile data may be removed or anonymized; financial, refund, booking, consent, fraud, and administrative-attribution records may require preservation under separately approved policies. Retained records must no longer grant login or ownership rights.

A deleted account must leave sufficient non-authenticating linkage or tombstone state to prevent a later Firebase identity—especially one reusing the same email—from inheriting the old local user, bookings, credits, messages, roles or administrator status. Recreated identities must be treated as new unless an explicit recovery procedure authorizes restoration.

Scheduled or event-driven reconciliation must detect Firebase users without local users, local users whose Firebase identities are missing or disabled, stale copied attributes, failed claim updates, and incomplete suspension/deletion operations. Automated repair must not reactivate or merge accounts without an unambiguous rule.

A valid Firebase token may establish `firebase_uid` only. Before any protected action, the backend must establish that a corresponding local user exists, the local state permits access, the current role/function permission permits the action, the actor has the required resource relationship, and the resource/workflow state permits the transition.

Authorization must deny by default and be validated on every request. Missing policy registration, unknown roles, null relationships, policy exceptions, database errors and cache failures must not fall through to allow.

Authorization logic must be expressed through consistently reused route dependencies, service/domain policy functions, query scopes, or a policy engine. The chosen design may vary, but scattered ad hoc conditionals must not be the sole mechanism for cross-cutting rules such as account state, administrator status or ownership.

Every endpoint accepting an object identifier must check authorization for the specific object and operation. UUIDs, obscurity, frontend ownership checks, possession of a related identifier, or prior authorization for another object are not sufficient.

Nested-resource access must verify both the child’s permission and its actual parent relationship. A URL such as `/games/A/messages/B` must not authorize message B merely because the caller may access game A or because B exists.

Relationship-based permissions—host, participant, waitlisted user, post owner, requester, chat member, notification recipient, payment owner, booking owner, uploader or assigned administrator—must be established from current server-side records, not client assertions or token claims.

Identity and ownership alone must not authorize an invalid state transition. The backend must check current states such as draft, published, active, completed, canceled, expired, hidden, removed, paid, refunded, waitlisted, promoted, suspended and pending deletion immediately before mutation.

Public, authenticated, owner, participant, host, administrator, financial-administrator, moderation and internal-operational functions must have explicit backend classifications. Hidden navigation, absent buttons, obscure paths, API documentation settings and frontend route guards are not authorization controls.

Debug, deprecated, maintenance, documentation and internal-operational routes must be removed from production or protected by an explicit policy appropriate to their function. A route’s undocumented or hidden status does not make it private.

Create and update inputs must use explicit allowlisted fields, with distinct schemas where privileges differ. Client input must not control role, administrator status, account status, ownership, user/admin IDs, hosting eligibility, provider IDs, payment/refund state, credit value, internal notes, moderation state, visibility, timestamps, deletion markers or audit metadata unless a specific authorized function permits that exact field.

PATCH and nested-object updates must map each accepted field explicitly and reject or safely ignore unknown fields according to a documented contract. Generic ORM construction or dictionary unpacking from untrusted request bodies into persistent models must not be used for privileged entities.

Response schemas must suppress fields the caller is not entitled to read. Internal notes, provider identifiers, private contact data, administrative metadata, payment details and hidden moderation data must not leak merely because the caller can access the containing object.

Queries should enforce actor, ownership, relationship, visibility, account state and soft-delete predicates as part of the database selection wherever feasible. Fetching an unrestricted row set and filtering only in the browser is prohibited; post-fetch backend checks remain necessary for complex transitions.

Lists, searches, lookups, counts, aggregates, joins, eager-loaded relations, exports and bulk endpoints must apply the same authorization scope as individual-object reads. Authorization must be checked for every submitted bulk identifier; partial success behavior must be explicit.

Pagination cursors must be opaque or integrity-protected and must not independently confer access. Changing, replaying or borrowing a cursor must never escape the caller’s current authorization scope or expose soft-deleted/hidden rows.

`401` must be used when valid authentication credentials are absent or unusable; `403` ordinarily indicates an authenticated actor lacks permission; `404` may conceal a private forbidden resource where existence itself is sensitive. Public-resource and administrator errors need not always be concealed, but behavior must be consistent for equivalent cases.

Authorization errors returned to clients must not disclose another user’s identity, ownership, internal state, policy predicates, or sensitive administrative reasons. Internally, failures may retain request correlation and policy identifiers without logging credentials or excessive private data.

Cached users, roles, relationships or permission results must have bounded staleness and invalidation for suspension, deletion, relationship removal, role removal and emergency administrator revocation. High-risk mutations must use current authoritative data at execution time rather than a stale cached decision.

High-impact or non-idempotent actions must recheck authorization and current state immediately before committing the side effect. Prior page access, preview authorization, or an earlier cached decision must not authorize later execution.

Authorization test coverage must include positive, negative, cross-user, cross-role, state-transition, field-injection, bulk, pagination, race and failure scenarios. Testing only unauthenticated access or happy paths is insufficient.

Every administrative request must require a valid Firebase ID token, current Firebase-account acceptability where revocation/disablement is relevant, an existing local user, an active non-deleting local state, and a current PostgreSQL administrator role or privilege. These conditions must be rechecked on every request.
Administrator privileges must be assigned to named personal identities. Shared administrator credentials and use of backend service accounts as interactive human administrators are prohibited.

A single administrator role may be used only where the number of administrators is small, duties are homogeneous, private-data and financial access are limited, and all members are approved for every administrative operation. Otherwise, separate at least read-only, user-management/moderation and financial privileges, with sensitive data access independently controlled.

All administrators must enroll an approved MFA factor before receiving or exercising administrative privileges. TOTP is preferable to SMS among Firebase-native options; phishing-resistant federation should be used for highest-impact administrators when feasible. MFA reset must itself be a high-risk verified process.

Administrator sessions must use an explicit shorter-risk posture than ordinary sessions: restricted persistence on shared/unmanaged devices, reauthentication after risk events, global revocation on device loss, and current role/state checks per request. A long-lived refreshable Firebase browser session must not be treated as perpetual proof of administrator presence.

Assigning/removing administrator privileges, deleting or restoring users, changing MFA/recovery, issuing refunds or credits, adjusting financial state, and accessing especially sensitive private data must require recent authentication or step-up. The backend must bind the step-up result to the acting administrator and a limited time window.

High-risk mutations must present the target and consequential values for confirmation, require an explicit reason where accountability or user impact warrants it, perform a final current-state and authorization check, and support safe retry through idempotency or equivalent duplicate detection.

Typed confirmation, preview, reversal windows, transaction limits, user notifications, dual control and second approval must be selected by risk. Dual control is strongly indicated for unusually large financial adjustments, granting top-level administrative access, destructive bulk actions, or access to exceptionally sensitive private data, but need not be imposed on routine low-risk moderation.

Only an already authorized privilege-management principal or approved bootstrap procedure may create administrators. Self-promotion through profile updates, custom claims, registration fields or ordinary admin APIs must be impossible. Administrator invitations must bind the approved person to the authenticated Firebase UID before privilege activation.

Initial administrator bootstrap must be one-time, narrowly controlled and disabled after use. The system must prevent accidental removal of the final usable administrator or require a separately tested recovery mechanism. Departing or reassigned administrators must be promptly offboarded from PostgreSQL, Firebase sessions and relevant Google Cloud access.

Administrator search must be access-controlled, rate- and result-limited, and return only fields needed for the task. Exact identifiers should be preferred for sensitive lookups; partial name/email search, deleted users, private contact details, bulk export and broad result sets require additional privilege or justification.

Access to private messages, payment-related data, recovery information, internal notes and support records must be separately justified and minimized. General administrator status must not automatically expose all such fields where duties do not require them.
classification: `STRONGLY RECOMMENDED`, becoming `REQUIRED` when duties are separated

text: Administrator impersonation should be absent unless a demonstrated support need exists. If enabled, it must use a separate time-limited mode with a persistent visible banner, acting-admin identity retained server-side, required reason, restricted operations, and prohibition on financial actions, role changes, credential changes and invisible impersonation.

Break-glass access is appropriate only where operational scale or availability needs justify it. If used, it must be a separate named emergency identity, protected by strong MFA, unavailable for routine use, narrowly privileged, securely recoverable, periodically tested, promptly rotated after use, and subject to post-use review.

Emergency privilege removal must update the authoritative PostgreSQL role or account state first, revoke Firebase refresh tokens, disable the Firebase identity when appropriate, invalidate authorization caches across instances, and remove relevant Google Cloud access. The procedure must be executable without cooperation from the affected administrator.

Maintain a distinct authoritative **administrative audit trail**. Access logs, application/error logs, moderation evidence, case events, financial ledgers, business-status history, and incident records may share correlation IDs but must not substitute for it.
Maintain a logging inventory that identifies event classes, fields, formats, destinations, writers, readers, uses, alerting, retention categories and failure behavior.

Record administrator authentication successes and failures, session elevation or break-glass use, and administrator authorization failures. Record successful sensitive-data access where the data category is private messages, payment context, moderation evidence, audit records or exports. Do not copy the sensitive payload into the access event.

Audit every consequential privileged mutation: role assignment/removal; suspension/restoration/deletion and deletion cancellation; hosting or participation restriction/restoration; content hide/remove/restore; game/post cancellation; chat action; case creation/state/resolution/reopen; note addition/correction; enforcement/reversal; refund/credit/adjustment/reconciliation; notice creation/scheduling/cancellation; and changes to security, access or retention configuration.

Record outcomes for significant failed, rejected or non-mutating attempts: authorization denial, invalid workflow state, stale version, duplicate/replayed request, same idempotency key with changed payload, provider rejection, database/audit failure and partial failure. Routine malformed public input may remain in security or operational logs unless it indicates abuse or affects a privileged operation.
classification: `REQUIRED` for privileged or security-relevant attempts; otherwise `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`

text: Each authoritative audit event must have an immutable unique event ID; authoritative UTC timestamp; event type; actor identifier and actor role/permission context; target type and ID; action; result; stable failure code where applicable; request/correlation ID; application/environment identity; and related case, enforcement, financial or notice identifiers when present.

Record selected structured state changes—such as old/new status, role, visibility, amount or assignment—rather than full object snapshots by default. Exclude secrets, tokens, raw private conversations, full payment data, unrestricted profile data and large request/response bodies.

Consequential actions must use a controlled reason code. Free-text explanation may be required by policy for selected actions, but must be bounded, safely rendered, validated as text, and accompanied by warnings against secrets, copied private messages, full payment data and irrelevant personal information. Do not impose arbitrary minimum text lengths.
classification: `STRONGLY RECOMMENDED`; `REQUIRED` where the action cannot otherwise be meaningfully reviewed

text: Audit events and action reasons must not be directly edited through ordinary application functionality. Corrections must be new linked annotation, superseding or corrective events that identify the original event, correcting actor, time and correction reason.

The application audit writer must have only the privileges necessary to append permitted events; ordinary application and administrator roles must lack audit `UPDATE` and `DELETE`. Audit reading and exporting must use separate permissions. The application must not connect as the audit-table owner or a PostgreSQL superuser.

Send an audit copy through a secure path to a logically separate security or audit system, or otherwise maintain an independently protected replica that the normal application writer cannot alter. Monitor forwarding failures and reconcile gaps.
classification: `STRONGLY RECOMMENDED`; `REQUIRED` where administrator compromise is in the threat model and the local application/database is not independently controlled

text: Cryptographic event signing, hash chaining, notarization and write-once storage require a documented risk decision. Use them when evidence must remain trustworthy against highly privileged database or infrastructure operators, or when external obligations require them. They are not universal requirements for this application.

For a local administrative mutation, create the authoritative audit event in the same transaction as the authoritative local state change where feasible. If provider actions or asynchronous pipelines prevent one transaction, use durable intent/result records, idempotent processing and reconciliation so neither business success nor audit loss is silent.
classification: `REQUIRED` for local authoritative state and event consistency; implementation form `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`

text: Use synchronized authoritative time, store UTC or explicit offset, distinguish event time from ingestion time when needed, and expose sequence/gap/duplicate indicators sufficient to detect delayed, duplicated or out-of-order events.

Build log records through structured field allowlists before emission. Redact at the source and logging boundary, including provider SDK logs, exception handling, HTTP access logs, query logging, frontend telemetry and error-monitoring systems. Post-storage scrubbing alone is insufficient.

Normalize, escape or encode untrusted log fields—including user content, excerpts, reasons, notes, user agents and provider errors—to prevent newline/control-character, terminal, HTML, JSON-delimiter and CSV/spreadsheet injection.

Audit search and viewing must be read-only, permission-scoped and paginated. Support searches by event ID, actor, target, event type, outcome, date/time, request/correlation ID and linked case/enforcement/financial/notice ID. Unbounded partial-text search over sensitive narratives is context-dependent.

Audit exports must require an export-specific permission, bounded query, purpose or reason, generated-file access control, secure transport/storage, expiration and deletion handling, export-event logging, and spreadsheet-formula protection. Recipient lists and unnecessary personal fields must be excluded by default.
classification: `REQUIRED` for export functionality; `NOT APPLICABLE UNDER STATED CONDITIONS` if no export is offered

text: Establish periodic and event-driven review of high-risk events. Candidate signals include role changes, break-glass access, private-message reads, audit exports, bulk actions, large or unusual financial changes, repeated failures, unusual access context and modification of logging/access configuration. Thresholds must be risk-derived, documented and tested rather than invented in this report.
classification: `REQUIRED` to define and perform review; exact thresholds `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`

text: Define retention by record purpose and data category, including active storage, archive, deletion/anonymization, legal hold, backups/snapshots, development copies and exports. Preserve stable attribution where needed while minimizing directly identifying fields for deleted users. No universal period is prescribed.
classification: `REQUIRED` to have and enforce a documented schedule; duration `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`

text: Maintain an owner-approved, versioned moderation taxonomy that maps detection rules and review outcomes to policy identifiers. The technical system must not infer the final policy merely from a keyword or model category.
classification: `REQUIRED` for consistent automated or manual moderation

text: Every deterministic or automated detection must identify detection type, rule/model/scanner ID and version, threshold or decision configuration, execution time, supported language/context limitations and provider where applicable.

Decide synchronously versus asynchronously, and fail-open versus fail-closed, by documented risk categories considering harm severity, exposure before review, reversibility, user latency, scanner reliability and backlog capacity. There is no universal choice.

A finding must identify the finding, target type/ID, target content version or immutable revision reference, field, rule/category/version, detection time, current/stale status, and links to case, review outcome and enforcement when present. Confidence, severity, offsets and excerpts are required only when the detector produces meaningful values.
classification: `REQUIRED` for core identity and lifecycle; optional fields `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`

text: Store the minimum evidence necessary for review: ordinarily a safely rendered excerpt plus bounded context and a source-version reference. Full content, full conversation, screenshots and attachments require a documented need and stronger access controls.
classification: `REQUIRED` as a minimization rule; precise evidence quantity `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`

text: When storing match spans, define whether offsets refer to bytes, Unicode code points or grapheme clusters and whether they apply to original or normalized text. Preserve enough mapping to highlight the correct original content safely.
classification: `STRONGLY RECOMMENDED` where spans are stored; otherwise `NOT APPLICABLE UNDER STATED CONDITIONS`

text: A content hash must declare canonicalization and hash-version rules. Hashes may support equality, duplicate detection and change comparison; they do not prove authorship, truth, policy violation or the time content existed. Unsalted hashes of predictable sensitive text require a privacy-risk decision.
classification: `STRONGLY RECOMMENDED` when hashes are used; hashing itself `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`

text: Define finding deduplication over target, field, content version/hash, rule or category, scanner version and active lifecycle state. Preserve `first_detected`, `last_detected` and occurrence count where repeated scans are collapsed. Do not collapse genuinely different rules merely because excerpts overlap.
classification: `REQUIRED` where rescanning or concurrent workers occur

text: Editing content must generate a new content version or otherwise change the comparison hash and trigger re-evaluation according to the content surface’s risk policy. Previous findings must be retained as historical and marked stale/non-current when they no longer match.

Staleness or deletion must not silently erase a case or enforcement history. Automatic closure or reversal is allowed only under a versioned policy that records the trigger and reason, checks current state, and supports review or reopening where appropriate.

Scanner timeout, outage, exception, invalid response, partial scan, queue failure and evidence-write failure must have an explicit non-clean state. Retry must be idempotent; exhausted or poison work must become visible to operators; backlog and failure conditions must be monitored.

If machine-learning classification is used, establish test/evaluation/validation/verification, threshold review, subgroup or language performance analysis, drift monitoring, model/version records and human-oversight criteria proportionate to impact.
classification: `REQUIRED` for production ML moderation governance; `NOT APPLICABLE UNDER STATED CONDITIONS` for deterministic-only moderation

text: Support flags must have category, target, source, priority, state, creation time, sensitivity, assignment and resolution data. Keep a flag separate from a moderation case when it is merely an operational observation or unvalidated signal; create/link a case only under documented triage rules.
Use an explicit server-enforced case state model that identifies permitted transitions, required inputs and terminal/nonterminal behavior. The exact state names are business-policy choices.

Case creation must be idempotent for the same trigger and use documented duplicate/merge rules. “One open case per target” must not be universal because one target may legitimately have different categories, reporters, time periods or risk owners.
Preserve distinct case priority, severity, category, target links, finding/signal/report links, assigned queue/user and creation reason. Do not infer severity solely from confidence score.

Case notes must distinguish internal-only from user-visible text; use server-side validation and safe rendering; restrict attachments; and prohibit direct editing/deletion through normal workflows. Corrections must be linked follow-up notes.

Maintain append-only case event history distinct from the current case row. Record creation, assignment/reassignment, links, notes, state/outcome changes, enforcement, reversal, target edit/deletion, resolution and reopen events.

Case resolution must record outcome code, reviewer or automation identity, timestamp, reason, evidence/finding references, linked enforcement if any, and user-notice status or suppression reason where applicable. Reopening must preserve—not replace—the prior resolution.

Concurrent reviewers must not silently overwrite one another. Use version preconditions, optimistic concurrency or locking, and return a conflict that exposes the refreshed non-sensitive current state. Duplicate notes or repeated resolution attempts must be idempotent or clearly rejected.

Assignment queues, reassignment, presence indicators, stale-assignment expiry, workload balancing and escalation should be selected according to team size and risk. Assignment must never substitute for authorization.

Automatic case resolution or merging must produce a case event and audit event identifying rule/version, trigger, old/new state and reason, and must handle concurrent human action through state preconditions.
classification: `REQUIRED` if automation exists; otherwise `NOT APPLICABLE UNDER STATED CONDITIONS`

text: Separation between investigator, recommender and executor, or dual approval, is required only for risk-defined high-impact operations such as exceptional financial adjustments, access to exceptionally sensitive information or irreversible mass action.
classification: `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`; may become `REQUIRED` for an organization’s high-assurance tier

text: Enforce action-specific permissions for suspend, restore, hide, remove, cancel, refund, credit, export, read-private-message and send-notice operations. A generic “administrator” role must not automatically confer every sensitive capability.

A consequential enforcement request must identify target, action, reason code, current expected state or version, actor, case/finding linkage where policy requires it, notice preference, and idempotency identifier where duplicate delivery is possible.

Idempotency must be scoped to the authenticated principal or service, operation and relevant target. Store a safe key representation plus request fingerprint. A completed duplicate with identical semantics returns the prior result; an in-flight duplicate returns conflict; reuse with materially different input is rejected and audited.
classification: `REQUIRED` for non-idempotent consequential operations exposed to retry; exact HTTP code `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`

text: Validate current target state, content version, ownership where relevant, case state and prior enforcement before acting. Already-applied equivalent actions may return the prior result; incompatible stale, deleted, restored, refunded or changed-version requests must return a conflict without mutation.

Local enforcement state and its authoritative audit event must commit consistently. External provider or financial side effects require explicit pending/succeeded/failed/unknown states, safe retries and reconciliation; do not mark provider success solely because a local request was accepted.

Reversible actions must preserve the original action and record a separate reversal/restoration with actor, reason, time, current-state validation and restored state. Never delete or rewrite the original enforcement row.

Identify irreversible or provider-limited actions before confirmation. Such actions require explicit confirmation and risk-appropriate permission; dual approval is context-dependent for the highest-impact cases.
classification: `REQUIRED` to identify and confirm irreversible effects; dual approval `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`

text: When moderation causes a refund, credit or adjustment, link the enforcement, financial operation, user/game target, amount/currency, provider reference, local/provider outcome and reconciliation status. Financial history remains a distinct ledger/history record linked to—not replaced by—the administrative audit event.

Generate a user-safe notice for enforcement when the application’s policy calls for one. It may identify affected content/action and a user-facing policy category, but must not expose secret rules, classifier thresholds, reporter identity, private third-party information, security telemetry or fraud-detection detail.
classification: `STRONGLY RECOMMENDED`; specific notice obligation and content `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`

text: Delaying or suppressing notice must require a structured reason under a documented safety, fraud, abuse, security or investigation policy. Restoration or reversal should generate a correction/restoration notice where the original action was communicated and the user remains reachable.
classification: `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`, but suppression rationale and auditability are `REQUIRED` when suppression is supported

text: Appeals are not established as a universal technical or legal requirement by the primary security sources used here. If the platform offers review or appeal, it must be a distinct case transition with new evidence, reviewer identity, reasoned result, enforcement linkage and conflict-safe restoration.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Maintain a data classification and task-to-field access matrix for contact data, birth dates, private messages, reports, moderation evidence, payment context, identity-provider data, device/IP data, support notes, deletion information and audit history.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Enforce minimum-necessary response fields at the backend. List/search pages must default to less detail than case-specific detail views. Frontend hiding or masking alone is not an authorization control.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Private-message access must be purpose-limited and normally case- or report-linked. Default to the reported message or relevant excerpt and bounded surrounding context. Full conversation access requires a more specific permission and recorded reason. All message-content reads must be audited; unrestricted bulk browsing must not exist.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Moderation evidence views must safely render text, minimize identity/contact/payment details irrelevant to the case, constrain context, and protect copying/export through permissions and audit. External links and attachments must not execute active content in the administrative interface.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Financial interfaces may show amount, currency, status, provider references, card brand and last four digits only where the task requires them. CVV/CVC, full track data and PIN/PIN-block data must never be stored or displayed after authorization. Full PAN must not be exposed in this administration system absent a separately justified PCI-scoped need.
classification: `REQUIRED` for sensitive-authentication-data prohibition and minimum necessary display; full-PAN handling `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT` but presumptively excluded

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Passwords, Firebase tokens, refresh tokens, authorization headers, cookies, API keys, webhook secrets, service-account credentials, private keys, presigned URLs, password-reset or verification links and sensitive authentication payloads must not be stored in audit records, notes, evidence or notices.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Administrative notes require controlled note types, safe text validation/rendering, access restrictions, retention classification, immutable creation metadata and linked correction. Warn and, where feasible, detect attempts to enter credentials, full card data, excessive private-message content, discriminatory or abusive language and irrelevant sensitive information.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Sensitive admin responses must use appropriate anti-caching controls, including `Cache-Control: no-store`, and sensitive data must not be deliberately persisted in localStorage, IndexedDB, analytics, frontend logs or client-side error reports. Clear sensitive client state on logout/session termination where feasible.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Progressive disclosure or temporary unmasking should require the task-appropriate permission and may require a reason for high-risk categories. The backend must return the unmasked value only after rechecking authorization; unmask actions for highly sensitive fields must be audited.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Clipboard disabling, print restrictions, watermarks and screenshot deterrence may be used for selected workflows but must not be represented as reliable prevention. Focus enforceable controls on backend access, export restriction, auditability, managed-device policy and operator accountability.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Sensitive list/search APIs must not return hidden fields “for convenience,” embed secrets in page source, preload unrelated messages/evidence, or include sensitive values in URLs. Browser autocomplete must be disabled where it could retain sensitive administrative entry.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Deleted-user audit attribution should normally retain a stable internal or pseudonymous subject reference while removing or minimizing direct identity fields according to the retention policy. Evidence required for open cases or security preservation must be access-restricted and explicitly retained.
classification: `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`, but the decision and enforcement are `REQUIRED`

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Model a notice campaign, immutable content version, audience definition/snapshot, recipient record and delivery attempt as distinct records. Maintain audit links to creator, approver where applicable, reason and cancellation/correction.
classification: `REQUIRED` for platform-wide or targeted administrative notices

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Notice creation must require category, title/body, internal reason, audience definition, content preview and explicit confirmation. High-risk categories or very large audiences may require separate approval under a documented threshold.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Define whether each campaign snapshots its audience at confirmation/scheduling time or evaluates eligibility at delivery time. Record the chosen semantics, preview count and snapshot/version. Establish explicit behavior for deleted, suspended, pending-deletion or newly ineligible users.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Deduplicate selected recipients by canonical internal user ID. Notice submission and recipient delivery must be idempotent. Reuse of the same key with changed campaign, audience or content must be rejected; a valid duplicate must return or reference the prior campaign/result.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Render notice content through a controlled plain-text, Markdown or sanitized-HTML pipeline; validate links and disallow scriptable content. Notices must not request credentials, include secrets, disclose private moderation/security detail or embed unnecessary recipient information.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Scheduled and queued notices need explicit states for draft, approved/scheduled, sending, partially sent, completed, canceled and failed or equivalent semantics. Cancellation must prevent unsent recipients where possible and record unavoidable in-flight delivery.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Do not edit content already sent to a recipient. Corrections or retractions must be new, linked notice versions/campaigns. Unsent drafts may be edited; scheduled approved content changes must invalidate or repeat approval as policy requires.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Track per-recipient states such as queued, sent, delivered where provider-confirmed, read where application-observed, skipped, failed, retried and canceled. Do not label a message “delivered” merely because it was accepted locally. Store stable normalized error codes and aggregate counts.

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Use queue/backpressure, recipient pagination, bounded concurrency and rate controls for large audiences. The campaign must expose progress and unresolved failures without loading or exporting the entire recipient list to every administrator.
classification: `STRONGLY RECOMMENDED`; `NOT APPLICABLE UNDER STATED CONDITIONS` for permanently small, bounded audiences

section: Sensitive administrative data and notice requirements
text: Enforcement, financial, maintenance, policy and security notices must use distinct templates and permissions. Security or fraud notices must be reviewed to avoid exposing exploitable internal details; financial notices must not contain raw payment credentials.
classification: `REQUIRED` for sensitive-content separation; template governance `STRONGLY RECOMMENDED`

text: Create and retain an engine/pool at process scope, but never permit live pooled DBAPI connections inherited from a parent process to be used by a forked child. Each child must create or reinitialize its own usable pool before database work.

Maintain a documented deployment-wide connection budget: `(maximum checked-out connections per process × API workers × application instances) + background-worker pools + administration/migration jobs + monitoring + operational reserve ≤ usable PostgreSQL connection capacity`. Count overflow, autoscaling maxima, rolling-deployment overlap, and proxy behavior.

Bound the number of checked-out and overflow connections and define finite pool-wait behavior. Pool exhaustion must fail predictably, release request resources, and not generate unbounded new connections.

Decide explicitly whether checkout validation, optimistic disconnect handling, age-based recycling, or an external pool/proxy supplies stale-connection protection. Test database restart and network interruption. `pre_ping` is strongly recommended when stale idle connections are plausible, but it cannot rescue a connection lost during an active transaction.

Initialize engines at a lifecycle point compatible with the process model and explicitly dispose them during graceful shutdown. Import-time creation is acceptable only when it cannot open or share unsafe connections before process initialization and credential/configuration loading.

Select synchronous or asynchronous SQLAlchemy consistently with the driver and workload. Never use `QueuePool` for an async engine; never share a `Session` or `AsyncSession` concurrently. Use one session per thread or asynchronous task.

Use a separately created session for each request, background-job attempt, webhook attempt, administrative operation, and migration context. Do not reuse request sessions in background tasks after the request has completed.

Every transactional session path must have deterministic success, exception, and cleanup behavior: commit only after the unit of work succeeds; roll back on exceptions; explicitly roll back after a failed flush before reuse; and close the session in all paths.

Treat `flush()` as sending pending changes and surfacing database errors inside the existing transaction, not as a durability boundary. User-visible success, job acknowledgement, and provider acknowledgement must not precede the required commit.

Do not keep a transaction open while awaiting user input, remote-provider calls, slow uploads, arbitrary sleeps, or a long streaming response. If lazy loading is needed after the session closes, materialize required data first or use an explicitly bounded read session.

Decide and document `expire_on_commit`, autoflush, and explicit-autobegin behavior. Any departure from defaults must have tests for stale objects, implicit queries, detached objects, and transaction start points.

Protect database URLs and credentials as secrets, require encrypted database transport where the network boundary is not otherwise trusted, redact credentials and sensitive bind values from logs, and design credential rotation so new connections use new credentials while old pools are retired.
classification: `REQUIRED` for secret protection and untrusted-network encryption; otherwise `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT` for exact TLS mode

text: Define a transaction around the smallest complete database invariant, not mechanically around an HTTP request. All database changes that must succeed or fail together must share one transaction; unrelated work may use separate transactions only when partial success is explicitly valid and recoverable.
Multiple commits in one business workflow require a documented intermediate state, idempotent continuation, recovery path, and user-visible semantics. Incidental helper-level commits are prohibited.

Never treat a database transaction and a remote provider call as one atomic transaction. Choose an explicit ordering and durable recovery design: transactional outbox for post-commit side effects, inbox/idempotency ledger for inbound events, or a staged saga with compensating action and reconciliation.

Store a durable idempotency key or immutable provider event/operation identifier under a unique constraint before or with the protected mutation. Replays must return or reconstruct the prior outcome rather than repeat a financial or allocation change.
classification: `REQUIRED` for retryable commands, webhooks, refunds, credits, provider operations, and jobs

text: Capacity-limited operations must use a database-enforced atomic decision: an atomic conditional update, lock of the authoritative capacity row followed by revalidation, exclusion/unique constraint where representable, or a serializable transaction with retry. A prior unlocked count is not sufficient.

Use the weakest row lock that protects the invariant. Lock rows in a consistent order, re-evaluate state after lock acquisition, and keep the lock-holding transaction short. Use `NOWAIT` only for immediate conflict semantics and `SKIP LOCKED` only where temporarily invisible locked rows are acceptable.

`SKIP LOCKED` may be used for multi-worker job claiming only when each job has a durable claim/status transition and eventual recovery of abandoned claims. It is inappropriate for user-facing listings, strict FIFO guarantees without further design, or any result requiring a consistent view of all eligible rows.

Use `READ COMMITTED` by default when each statement operates on explicit rows and constraints/atomic updates protect invariants. Use repeatable read for a stable transaction snapshot when serialization anomalies are acceptable or otherwise prevented. Use serializable for cross-row or predicate invariants when its retry and overhead model is acceptable.

Implement optimistic concurrency with a monotonic version value or another unambiguous compare-and-swap predicate and verify the affected-row count. Return a conflict rather than silently overwriting stale administrative, moderation, profile, or game edits.

Do not rely on `updated_at` alone for optimistic concurrency unless its precision, source, mutation coverage, and equality semantics make collisions impossible for the workload. Prefer a dedicated incrementing version where correctness depends on detecting every write.

Catch and retry only errors classified as transient for the whole transaction, including deadlock victims and serialization failures. Retries must be bounded, use backoff/jitter where contention could synchronize workers, and re-run from a clean session with the same idempotency identity.
classification: `REQUIRED` where deadlock or stronger-isolation retries are expected

text: Select `statement_timeout`, `lock_timeout`, `transaction_timeout`, and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` by workload class and validate them against legitimate operations. Do not use one arbitrary global value for requests, migrations, backfills, reports, and workers.

Audit records needed to prove the committed business change should normally be inserted in the same transaction. Delivery notifications and external communications should normally be represented by an outbox record in that transaction and delivered after commit.

Savepoints may isolate expected per-item failures inside a larger transaction, but code must use the nested transaction handle correctly and understand that `Session.commit()` commits the outermost transaction in SQLAlchemy 2.0. Savepoints are not a substitute for idempotency or workflow-level recovery.

Bulk operations must define batching, transaction size, retry granularity, idempotency, validation, audit behavior, and ORM-state synchronization. Avoid one transaction whose lock duration, WAL volume, memory, or rollback cost has not been tested at production scale.

Every persistent entity must have a stable primary key; every required relationship must have a foreign key; logically required scalar values must be `NOT NULL`. Application validation alone is insufficient for writes from workers, migrations, administration, or concurrent code paths.

Enforce race-sensitive identity rules with unique constraints or unique indexes. Use composites for scoped identity and partial unique indexes for “one active/open row” only after the business predicate is defined. Explicitly decide null and soft-delete semantics.
classification: `REQUIRED` when duplicate rows would violate integrity; otherwise `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`

text: Enforce row-local invariants with check constraints: nonnegative or positive amounts where policy requires, valid ranges, end after start, permitted field combinations, conditional required fields, and coherent status/timestamp combinations. Do not use a check constraint to inspect mutable data in other rows.

Select `CASCADE`, `RESTRICT`/`NO ACTION`, or `SET NULL` per relationship and historical requirement. Financial records, provider records, moderation findings, messages, and audit attribution must not be physically erased merely because a user, game, or venue is deleted unless an approved retention model explicitly permits it.

Use database/server defaults for values that must be valid for every insertion path, including server-generated timestamps and stable initial states. ORM defaults may improve ergonomics but must not be the sole protection.

Store money using either integer minor units with an explicit currency and unit contract, or exact `numeric` with justified precision/scale and a documented rounding policy. Do not use binary floating-point for authoritative monetary values. Preserve immutable historical gross, fee, tax, refund, and provider amounts needed for reconciliation.

Store instants such as creation, payment, expiration, and delivery times as `timestamp with time zone` and exchange them in an unambiguous offset/UTC representation. Store date-only concepts as `date`. Preserve venue local time zone and local scheduling intent where recurrence or civil-time reconstruction requires it. Test ambiguous and nonexistent daylight-saving times.

Adopt soft deletion only where restoration, historical linkage, review, or delayed cleanup requires it. Use one unambiguous representation, ensure every ordinary query applies the visibility predicate, adapt uniqueness with partial indexes or retained identity rules, and test restoration and accidental visibility.

Choose PostgreSQL enums, check constraints, or lookup tables based on evolution needs. Stable closed values may use enums; frequently changing states generally favor checks or lookup tables. Regardless of representation, application acceptance and database enforcement must remain compatible during rolling deployments.

Treat extension installation and version changes as migrations.
