Verify availability, privileges, version, managed-service support, environment parity, upgrade behavior, and reversibility before depending on `pgcrypto`, `citext`, `uuid-ossp`, `pg_trgm`, or other extensions. No listed extension is automatically required.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Add non-constraint indexes only for demonstrated query, sorting, join, or maintenance patterns. Evidence must include representative SQL, data distribution, plan, frequency, latency/resource objective, and measured improvement.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Evaluate indexes on foreign-key referencing columns and frequent relation lookups, but do not assume PostgreSQL creates them automatically. Add them where delete/update checks, joins, or filtering demonstrate need.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Design multicolumn indexes around actual equality, range, and ordering predicates; verify column order. Use partial indexes only when query predicates reliably imply the index predicate, and expression indexes for stable normalized lookups such as case-folded email where justified.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Use B-tree for ordinary equality/range/order cases unless another access method is demonstrated. GIN, GiST, trigram, and full-text capabilities require a defined operator/query pattern, extension availability where applicable, write-cost evaluation, and production-like plan tests.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Review critical queries with `EXPLAIN`; use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` only where executing the statement is safe, preferably in a controlled environment or inside a rollbackable transaction when side effects are fully understood. Include buffers and actual-versus-estimated rows where needed.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Establish ORM query budgets for high-volume paths and test for N+1 loading. Choose lazy, select-in, joined, or explicit projection loading based on cardinality and response needs; avoid materializing large object graphs or columns not returned.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Verify that autovacuum and statistics collection are enabled and effective, and monitor stale statistics, dead tuples, long transactions, and query-level execution data. Consider `pg_stat_statements` only after confirming extension availability, privacy implications, and configuration.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Use keyset/cursor pagination for large or frequently changing ordered datasets when deep offsets would be expensive or inconsistent. The order must be total and stable, normally business sort columns plus a unique tie-breaker; cursor filters must reproduce that lexicographic order.
classification: `STRONGLY RECOMMENDED` for large mutable feeds; otherwise `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Cursor contents must be validated against allowed sort/filter context and protected against undetected tampering when they carry authoritative continuation state. A cursor must not permit arbitrary SQL identifiers or bypass authorization filters.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Build indexes on live large tables using a rehearsed method that accounts for lock behavior. `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` reduces write blocking but has special transaction and failure behavior; detect and remediate invalid indexes after failure.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Bind every untrusted scalar value through SQLAlchemy/driver parameters, including textual SQL. Do not construct SQL by concatenating user input, including search values, JSON values, or migration data.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Dynamic identifiers and syntax that cannot be bind parameters—column names, table names, operators, sort direction, selected JSON path structure—must be chosen from a fixed application allowlist or constructed with trusted SQLAlchemy/Psycopg identifier APIs.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: The runtime application role must not be a PostgreSQL superuser, database owner, schema owner, or unrestricted migration role. Grant only the object and sequence privileges required by runtime operations.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Separate runtime, migration/DDL, read-only reporting, and emergency administration capabilities where their privileges differ. A separate background-worker role is required only when workers genuinely need a different privilege set.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Revoke unneeded `CREATE` privileges on application-visible schemas, control ownership and default privileges, and configure a trusted `search_path`. Do not place schemas writable by untrusted roles ahead of trusted schemas.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Redact credentials, tokens, personal data, payment metadata, and sensitive bind values from SQL, connection, exception, and migration logs. Error responses must not expose raw database statements, schema details, or credentials.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Consider row-level security only when database-enforced row scoping provides meaningful defense across trusted application paths. If used, test owner and `BYPASSRLS` behavior, policy coverage for every command, migration effects, and operational/reporting access.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Keep development, test, staging, and production credentials and databases separate. Direct developer production access must be time-bounded, attributable, least privileged, and governed by an emergency-access process.

section: Query, indexing, pagination, and database-security requirements
text: Extension creation and privileged functions must be restricted to approved migration/administrative roles. Review function execution privileges and security-definer behavior where custom functions exist.

Maintain an intentional Alembic revision DAG. Production deployment must identify the expected head or heads; accidental branches must be merged or explicitly supported. Do not edit an already-applied revision to change production history.

Manually review every generated migration against the intended schema and PostgreSQL operational behavior. Verify names, types, defaults, constraints, indexes, destructive operations, server expressions, extension dependencies, and data preservation.

Use expand-and-contract for changes incompatible with concurrently running old code: add compatible structures, deploy code able to use both forms, backfill/dual-write as needed, switch reads, stop old writers, and only then remove obsolete structures.
classification: `REQUIRED` for rolling deployments or independently deployed workers

text: Add a new required column to populated data through a rehearsed staged sequence: add it in a compatible form, backfill existing rows, validate completeness, arrange a safe default/write path, then enforce `NOT NULL`. Do not assume one-step alteration is safe for a large table.
classification: `STRONGLY RECOMMENDED`; `REQUIRED` where old rows or old writers exist

text: For new foreign keys or large-table constraints, separate creation and validation where PostgreSQL supports it and where lock/rewrite risk justifies the complexity. Validate existing data before declaring completion.

Create large production indexes with the appropriate online strategy. When using PostgreSQL concurrent index creation, run it outside transaction contexts that prohibit it, monitor both phases, and detect invalid indexes left by failure before retrying or attaching a constraint.

Treat long data backfills as resumable jobs unless a single migration transaction has been proven safe at production scale. Batch by a stable key, record progress, make updates idempotent, validate counts and invariants, and tolerate interruption.

Test upgrades from both an empty database and a production-like current schema. Also test the full migration chain, expected heads, model/schema comparison, data preservation, constraints, indexes, extension parity, and the exact PostgreSQL major version intended for production.

Every migration requires a recovery classification: transactionally reversible, safely downgradeable, forward-fix only, or recoverable only through restore/rebuild. A downgrade is not required when reversal would be destructive or misleading, but irreversibility must be explicit and rehearsed.

Ensure only one coordinated migration execution changes a database lineage at a time, and verify the live Alembic revision before and after deployment. Do not allow competing deployers to race DDL or version-table updates.

Verify extension, collation, encoding, PostgreSQL version, and Alembic/driver parity across development, CI, staging, and production. Migration behavior must be tested against PostgreSQL rather than inferred from SQLite or another database.

Renames, type changes, enum changes, drops, and table rewrites require explicit compatibility and lock analysis. Destructive cleanup must occur only after old application versions, jobs, webhooks, and rollback paths no longer use the old structure.

Alembic environment loading must avoid unintended application startup side effects, remote calls, worker creation, or writes. Metadata imports must be deterministic and complete, including multiple metadata collections where intentionally used.
Name constraints and indexes deterministically so that migrations can refer to, alter, and drop them reliably across environments.
The server must derive the charge amount and currency from trusted booking, pricing, and credit data; client-supplied totals may be advisory only and must be recomputed.

Each logical checkout must have a durable local operation identity linked to at most one active PaymentIntent unless an explicitly recorded replacement occurs. Reuse an existing Intent for a resumed checkout when amount, currency, customer, and business purpose remain compatible.

PaymentIntent creation and other Stripe POST mutations must use a stable idempotency key tied to the business operation and retained locally through retries. A key must never be reused for a materially different parameter set.

Stripe idempotency must be supplemented by local uniqueness and operation-state controls. The database must prevent two local payments, refunds, or administrative actions from representing the same logical operation.

A PaymentIntent client secret may be returned only to the authenticated and authorized user associated with that checkout. It must not be logged, embedded in URLs, stored in analytics, included in support screenshots, or exposed to another user.

Publishable keys may appear in the frontend. Secret and restricted keys must remain server-side. Webhook signing secrets are separate per endpoint and environment and must not be treated as API keys or exposed to clients.

The Payment Element may collect and tokenize payment information and drive confirmation/authentication, but the backend must create or authorize payment objects and independently establish the final application result.

A return URL or client callback must never be the sole trigger for marking a booking paid, issuing a credit, sending an official paid-game confirmation, or performing another irreversible entitlement action.

The webhook endpoint must verify the `Stripe-Signature` using the endpoint’s signing secret and the exact raw request bytes before JSON transformation or business processing. Invalid signatures must not create durable financial effects.
IP allowlisting, when used, must remain defense in depth and must not replace signature verification.

Webhook ingestion must keep a ledger keyed by Stripe event ID, recording event type, API version, object ID, receipt time, processing status, attempt count, last error, and completion time. The event ID must be unique locally.

Event handlers must tolerate out-of-order and delayed events. When correctness depends on current state, retrieve the relevant Stripe object or compare provider state and timestamps instead of assuming arrival order.

Webhook ingress should authenticate, validate basic structure, durably record the event, and acknowledge promptly; lengthy provider calls, notifications, reconciliation, and image-independent business work should be deferred to durable processing.

Stripe connection errors, API errors, and timeouts without a definitive response must be recorded as indeterminate, not assumed failed. Retry with the same idempotency key where permitted, then resolve through retrieval, webhook state, or reconciliation.

API version, SDK version, webhook endpoint version, and deserialization assumptions must be explicitly recorded and tested. Version changes must use a staged migration rather than silently changing live payload structure.
Test and live mode credentials, Customers, PaymentIntents, PaymentMethods, webhook endpoints, signing secrets, and operational dashboards must remain unambiguously separated.

Secret keys should be stored in a secret-management facility, restricted by resource and stable egress IP where feasible, periodically rotated, monitored in request logs, and immediately revoked after suspected exposure.

Payment methods saved for future use must be attached through a Customer-aware PaymentIntent/SetupIntent flow and associated locally with the owning application user. A method attached to another Customer must not be usable by the requester.

Saving a method must be an explicit product decision with appropriate user disclosure and future-use configuration. Use SetupIntents for setup without payment or `setup_future_usage` when saving during payment, subject to supported payment-method behavior.
classification: `REQUIRED` when saving methods; otherwise `NOT APPLICABLE UNDER STATED CONDITIONS`

text: Local saved-method data must be limited to identifiers and display metadata needed by the application—such as Stripe Customer and PaymentMethod IDs, type, brand, last four digits, expiry, and selected billing-display data. Full primary account numbers, CVC values, secret keys, or raw sensitive payment payloads must not be stored or logged.

Local payment-method metadata must be treated as a cache. Before a sensitive use, verify ownership and current Stripe state; handle detached, replaced, expired, or deleted methods without trusting stale local display data.

Logs may contain Stripe object IDs, event IDs, status, amount, currency, Stripe request ID, local correlation ID, redacted idempotency fingerprint, and error class. Logs must exclude secrets, full client secrets, Authorization headers, card/CVC data, and unredacted raw payloads containing unnecessary personal data.

Stripe Dashboard launch review must verify live/test mode, webhook URL and version, enabled event categories, recent delivery health, API/request logs, payment-method configuration, team roles, MFA, restricted-key scopes, and dispute notifications without recording secret values.
Subscribe only to event categories required by the implemented payment, refund, saved-method, and dispute flows. Unknown events must be safely recorded or ignored without failing the whole endpoint.

The PaymentIntent is the primary Stripe payment-lifecycle object. Charges may be retained as attempt/settlement references, but local payment status must not be inferred from “a Charge exists” when the PaymentIntent is nonterminal or has multiple attempts.

PostgreSQL must be authoritative for booking status, capacity, application-credit ledger, administrative reason, and user-visible financial history. Stripe remains authoritative for Stripe payment, refund, PaymentMethod, Customer, and dispute state.

Local state must include a non-success representation for payment states such as awaiting method, awaiting confirmation/action, processing, failed, canceled, and provider outcome unknown. Unsupported provider states must not default to success.

A synchronous Stripe response and a webhook may race. Both paths must call the same idempotent transition rules or otherwise use database concurrency controls so an older observation cannot overwrite a newer authoritative state.
Provider timestamps, local observation timestamps, event IDs, and object IDs must be retained sufficiently to explain ordering and prevent blind last-writer-wins updates.

The booking-versus-payment sequence must use one documented policy: pending booking with capacity hold, booking after confirmed payment, or another compensating design. No design may assume atomic commit across Stripe and PostgreSQL.
Capacity reservation and checkout creation must be concurrency-safe. Multiple simultaneous checkouts for the same user or last available place must not each create independent confirmed entitlements.

When Stripe succeeds but the local booking transaction fails, the system must preserve the provider identifiers and mark the operation unresolved for retry, compensation, refund, credit, or operator review; it must never discard evidence of the successful payment.

When local preparation succeeds but Stripe fails definitively, the local reservation or pending booking must be released, expired, or remain explicitly unpaid according to policy. It must not be presented as paid.

A booking canceled while payment is processing must remain in an explicit race-resolution state until the payment reaches a provider outcome; if payment later succeeds, the configured compensation path must run exactly once.

Every refund request must reference a specific local payment and Stripe payment/charge, validate currency and amount against the current remaining refundable amount, and carry a unique business-operation key.

A local refund record should be created as requested/pending before or atomically with durable scheduling of the provider action; provider success, pending, failure, and unknown outcome must be represented separately.

If the refund provider call succeeds but the local commit fails, retry/retrieve with the same operation identity and reconcile the Stripe Refund before creating another. If local state commits but provider execution fails, retain a failed or unresolved operation rather than marking refunded.

Application credits should be represented by an append-only or correction-based ledger of issuance, spend, reversal, expiration, refund-to-credit, promotion, and administrative adjustment. A mutable balance alone is insufficient as the sole record.

Credit issuance, spend, reversal, and refund-to-credit operations must have unique idempotency keys and immutable links to their originating booking, payment, cancellation, promotion, or administrative action.
Concurrent credit spending must lock or atomically condition the spend against the available balance. A read-then-write sequence without concurrency control is prohibited.
Amounts must use exact decimal or integer-minor-unit representation together with an explicit currency; binary floating-point must not be used for financial balances or refund arithmetic.

Whether negative balances, transferability, expiration, mixed credit/card tender, and partial credit use are permitted must be explicit product policy enforced by constraints and tests, not emergent behavior.

Administrative financial actions must require least-privilege authorization, current-state revalidation, a reason, preview of amount/currency/effect, explicit confirmation, operation idempotency, and an immutable audit record.

MFA or recent reauthentication should protect privileged financial administration. Phishing-resistant authenticators should be favored for higher-risk staff. Separation of duties or dual approval is context-dependent based on transaction value and organizational risk.

Manual status correction must not rewrite provider history to fabricate a Stripe outcome. It should record an override or resolution with actor, reason, prior value, evidence, and reconciliation disposition.

Dispute events and current Dispute objects must update a local dispute record and trigger administrative review. Booking and credit effects must follow explicit policy rather than automatically assuming the original payment never existed.

Reconciliation must compare Stripe PaymentIntents, Charges where needed, Refunds, and Disputes with local payments, refunds, bookings, and credits. It must detect missing records, amount/currency/status mismatches, duplicate mappings, and unresolved operations.

Reconciliation must paginate provider results, observe API limits, checkpoint progress, and be safely resumable. Frequency must be selected from transaction volume, asynchronous payment methods, dispute exposure, financial materiality, and staffing rather than a universal interval.
User notifications with financial meaning must be generated from committed state through a transactional outbox or equivalent durable mechanism and must be idempotent.
classification: `STRONGLY RECOMMENDED`; `REQUIRED` where notice is part of a financial promise

text: R2 credentials must remain server-side or in trusted workers. Browser uploads must use presigned URLs or temporary scoped credentials rather than long-lived Access Key ID/Secret Access Key pairs.

Each service token must use the least R2 permission and narrowest bucket scope that supports its role. Read-only delivery, upload/processing, deletion, and configuration administration should not automatically share one broad credential.
classification: `STRONGLY RECOMMENDED`; `REQUIRED` where broad scope is unnecessary

text: Development, test, and production objects must be separated by distinct buckets or equivalently strong account/bucket controls. Production credentials must not be used in local development or CI jobs that do not need production data.
Buckets must remain private unless a documented object category is intentionally public. Public access through `r2.dev` must not be used for production delivery.

Private moderation evidence, identity-related images, attachments not intended for global publication, abandoned uploads, unvalidated originals, and deleted/hidden content must never be public by default.

Object keys must be generated by the backend, collision-resistant, and bound to an authorized owner/category. User filenames may be stored as sanitized display metadata but must not control the actual key or path.

Object keys should avoid personal data and stable sensitive identifiers where not operationally necessary. Environment and object-category prefixes are permissible, but authorization must not depend on key secrecy.
Overwriting an existing key must be prohibited for untrusted direct uploads unless replacement is an explicit, concurrency-controlled operation. Prefer immutable/versioned keys for published assets.

A presigned URL must be issued only after authenticating the user, authorizing the object category and owner, creating the object key server-side, and applying the application’s configured upload limits.

Presigned URLs must be method-, bucket-, and object-key-specific and use the shortest expiry compatible with the workflow. Signed `Content-Type` may be used as a preliminary constraint, but it is not content validation.

Presigned URLs must be treated as bearer secrets and excluded from logs, analytics, support transcripts, referrer-bearing links, and persistent client storage. The same URL may be replayed until it expires; it is not inherently one-time-use or immediately revocable.
Browser access to presigned or custom-domain R2 endpoints must use a narrow CORS policy listing intended production origins, methods, and headers. CORS is not an authorization control.
Direct-upload workflows must create a durable upload-session record before issuing authorization, including owner, intended category, object key, expected type/limit policy, expiry, and status.

Client claims that an upload completed must be treated as a request to verify, not as proof. The backend or worker must perform `HEAD`/read checks for the expected key, size, metadata, and, where used, checksum/ETag before linking or publishing.
An uploaded object must remain in an unvalidated, private, or quarantine state until file validation and required image processing succeed. Publication must be a separate state transition.

Validation must use defense in depth: allowlisted extension where filenames are accepted, declared MIME check, independent signature/magic-byte check, and full image decoding. No single check may be treated as sufficient.

The application must define business-appropriate byte-size, width, height, total-pixel, frame-count, and processing-time limits. Exact values are product/workload decisions, but enforcement before publication is mandatory.
Image processing must run with memory, disk, CPU/runtime, dimension, and sequence/frame limits and with unnecessary external delegates or dangerous coders disabled.
SVG must be rejected, sanitized by a purpose-built process, or rendered into a safe raster form before public use. Serving arbitrary user SVG inline as ordinary trusted imagery is not acceptable.
Animated/multi-frame images must be explicitly accepted or rejected. If accepted, frame count, aggregate decoded size, processing time, and output behavior must be bounded.
classification: `REQUIRED` when animation is accepted; otherwise reject

text: Re-encoding validated raster images and stripping unnecessary EXIF and other metadata is strongly recommended for public profile and venue images. Orientation should be normalized before metadata removal.

Antivirus or malware scanning is risk-based rather than universally mandatory for a tightly constrained decode-and-reencode raster-only workflow. It becomes strongly indicated when originals are retained/downloadable, broad formats are accepted, or files may be passed to other parsers.

Database image records must track owner, category, original key if retained, derived keys, validation state, visibility, byte size, detected type, hash/ETag where useful, creation/update times, and deletion state. Provider metadata alone must not encode application authorization.
Original and derived objects must have explicit relationships. A thumbnail failure must not silently mark the image fully published if required derivatives are absent.

Published responses must send the detected output `Content-Type`, appropriate `Content-Disposition`, and cache policy. User-provided metadata must not control unsafe response headers. `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` should be applied at the delivery layer.

Published assets should use immutable/versioned object keys with long-lived caching where appropriate. Replacing bytes under one public key requires explicit cache-purge handling and should not be the default.
Deletion must be a durable state transition covering original and all derived objects. Missing objects should be treated idempotently; failed deletions must be retryable and visible to operations.

When a publicly cached object is removed or hidden, the system must use a new key strategy or purge/invalidate the relevant cache when immediate removal is required. R2 deletion alone does not guarantee immediate disappearance from a custom-domain cache.
classification: `REQUIRED` where immediate public revocation is required

text: Orphan detection must compare upload sessions and database image records with R2 listings/checks and classify abandoned objects, rows without objects, objects without rows, failed derivatives, and deleted-owner content.

Orphan cleanup must use a product-approved grace period, dry run or quarantine for ambiguous cases, idempotent deletion, pagination/checkpointing, and an operator-visible report. No universal cleanup age is prescribed.

R2 lifecycle rules may expire temporary or abandoned-object prefixes, but lifecycle timing is asynchronous and must not replace application state reconciliation. Retention periods require explicit product/legal decisions.

R2 Dashboard review must verify bucket inventory, public access, custom domains, CORS, lifecycle and lock rules, token scopes, environment separation, object/storage trends, and credential-rotation ownership without exposing credential values.

Financial actions, webhook processing after acknowledgement, image validation, reconciliation, orphan cleanup, account deletion, and other work that must survive process failure must use a durable database-backed queue or dedicated/managed queue—not only FastAPI `BackgroundTasks`.
In-process background tasks are acceptable only for best-effort, noncritical work whose loss on process termination is explicitly acceptable and which does not require multi-instance coordination.
classification: `NOT APPLICABLE UNDER STATED CONDITIONS` for financial/storage consistency work; otherwise `CONTEXT-DEPENDENT`

text: A durable job record must include a unique ID, job type and schema version, status, available time, attempt count, creation/update timestamps, and a payload or durable payload reference.

Jobs requiring exclusive processing must additionally track claim/lease owner, claim time, lease expiry or visibility timeout, start/completion/failure times, last error, and correlation/operation key.
Priority, maximum-attempt policy, heartbeat, deadline, and dead-letter fields are conditional on workload needs, but their absence must be deliberate. Payload data sensitivity must be documented.

Database-backed workers must claim jobs atomically. `SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` inside a short transaction is an appropriate PostgreSQL mechanism for queue-like tables, provided status/lease updates occur in the same transaction.
Row locking during claim is not a substitute for an execution lease. The claim transaction should be short; external provider calls must not hold long database locks.

Lease duration must exceed normal processing time or be renewed by heartbeat for long jobs. Lease expiry must make the job reclaimable, with the handler remaining safe if the original worker later resumes.

Job handlers must assume at-least-once execution. “Exactly once” may describe a queue feature but does not remove the need for idempotent application side effects across databases and external providers.
Each side-effecting job must have a business idempotency identity enforced by database uniqueness or a durable side-effect marker, plus provider idempotency where available.
A handler must record sufficient intermediate state to determine whether a partial operation can be resumed, safely repeated, compensated, or reconciled.
A database change that must reliably cause a job, notification, or queue message should write an outbox/job row in the same PostgreSQL transaction as the domain change.
Outbox dispatch and downstream consumption must remain idempotent because a dispatcher can publish a message and crash before marking it sent.

Retry policy must classify failures: transient network/5xx/rate-limit failures may retry; invalid payload, authorization failure, unsupported version, and invariant violations normally require correction or dead-letter handling.
Automatic retries should use increasing backoff and jitter and honor provider `Retry-After` or rate-limit guidance where available. No single retry count or window applies to all job types.

A network timeout after a provider call must be handled as unknown outcome. The next attempt must use the same provider idempotency key or retrieve/reconcile the provider object before issuing another mutation.
Maximum attempts and retry windows must be selected per job class based on provider behavior, user harm, deadlines, and operator coverage. Exhaustion must not silently discard the job.
Exhausted, invalid, repeatedly crashing, unsupported-version, or permanently provider-rejected jobs must enter a dead-letter/unresolved state visible to operators with redacted error context.

Manual replay must revalidate current state, preserve the original job and audit trail, create a new attempt identity, and retain the same business idempotency identity where the operation is the same. Bulk retry requires safeguards against duplicate side effects.

Job execution timeouts and provider/database timeouts must be distinct. Timeout should cancel or terminate local work safely, release/recover the lease, and preserve unknown provider outcomes for reconciliation.

Image-processing jobs should execute in an isolated process/container with hard resource limits so terminating a malicious or runaway decoder does not terminate unrelated API requests or financial workers.

Scheduled jobs must prevent duplicate logical runs through a unique schedule-run key, database advisory lock, leader election, or equivalent. The job itself must remain idempotent because scheduler coordination can fail.
Scheduled-run policy must define time zone, daylight-saving behavior, missed-run catch-up, overlap, and maximum tolerated lateness. These values are workload decisions.

Job payloads must not contain Stripe secret keys, webhook secrets, full client secrets, Firebase tokens, raw card data, or unnecessarily persistent presigned URLs. Prefer database/provider references over duplicated sensitive payloads.

Job payloads must be schema-versioned. Workers must reject or dead-letter unsupported future versions rather than interpreting them incorrectly. Rolling deployment must ensure producers do not emit versions older workers cannot safely process.

Workers must support graceful shutdown: stop claiming new jobs, complete or safely checkpoint in-flight work within a bounded period, and allow expired leases to be reclaimed after forced termination.

Worker health must expose at least queue depth or pending count, oldest pending age, claim/processing rate, retry rate, failure rate, dead-letter count, lease-expiry count, and worker version. Thresholds are workload-specific.
Priority queues must prevent indefinite starvation of lower-priority work. Batch claiming must be bounded so one worker cannot monopolize the queue.

All deployable frontend artifacts must be produced by a successful `vite build` or an equivalently configured production build. The development server and `vite preview` must not serve production traffic.

CI must select and record the intended Vite mode and must validate that mode, `NODE_ENV`, API base URL, environment identifier, and feature-flag inputs are mutually consistent. Invalid or missing mandatory values must fail the build.

The built artifact must be inspected—not merely the source configuration—for forbidden credentials, development endpoints, localhost references, unintended environment names, and live/test provider mismatches before release.

The application must have a documented browser-support policy, and Vite `build.target`, polyfills, and automated browser coverage must be consistent with it. Default Vite targets may be accepted only after confirming that the product policy matches them.

Base paths, asset URLs, and history fallback must be validated for every deployment environment. Direct navigation and refresh of each supported client route must produce the application or an intentional server error page—not an accidental object-store 404.

Every Effect that allocates a subscription, event listener, timer, connection, observer, or network operation must release or cancel it during cleanup, and cleanup must be safe when setup is repeated.

Requests whose results are no longer relevant must be aborted or logically ignored through sequence identity, cache identity, or equivalent stale-result protection. Navigation, filter changes, logout, and identity changes must invalidate pending work.

List keys must represent stable domain identity and must not depend on array position where ordering, insertion, deletion, or filtering can occur. Intentional state reset must use an explicit identity boundary.

Inputs must maintain a deliberate controlled or uncontrolled lifecycle and must not unexpectedly switch modes. Server-generated, disabled, read-only, and hidden values must not be treated as trustworthy user authority.

Render-time failures in major route or feature boundaries must be contained by an error boundary or router-equivalent recovery boundary. Separate handling must exist for event-handler, asynchronous, request, and provider failures, which ordinary React error boundaries do not catch automatically.

API communication must use a shared contract layer that consistently applies the base URL, bearer token, timeout/cancellation policy, request identifier, content-type handling, and normalized error categories.

Retry policy must distinguish safe/idempotent reads from mutations. Automatic mutation retry is prohibited unless the operation is idempotent by protocol or protected by a server-recognized idempotency key. Backoff must honor explicit rate-limit information where available.

Application caches must distinguish server state from local UI state and use identity-, role-, resource-, filter-, and environment-specific cache keys. Mutations must invalidate or update affected entries, and logout or user change must clear user-scoped state.

Every asynchronous screen and mutation must define initial-loading, background-refresh, empty, stale, retryable-error, permanent-error, unauthorized, deleted/hidden-resource, offline/network, and completion behavior as applicable. An indefinite spinner without timeout or recovery path is noncompliant.

Chunk-load and dynamic-import failure handling must offer a bounded recovery path, normally a one-time reload or navigation to a stable shell, without entering a reload loop. Releases must use cacheable fingerprinted assets and an entry document caching strategy that does not indefinitely reference deleted chunks.

Production source-map handling must be an explicit release decision. Public maps must be treated as public source disclosure; private maps must be access-controlled, associated with a release, uploaded without credentials, and retained only as needed.

Images must declare intrinsic dimensions or an equivalent aspect ratio, use responsive sources where appropriate, lazy-load noncritical content, prioritize the actual LCP image, provide alternative text according to purpose, and handle missing or expired objects without breaking layout.

Component and state boundaries must follow change ownership: transient UI state remains local; server state uses a query/cache boundary; authentication and environment state have explicit providers; global mutable state may be introduced only for documented cross-feature requirements.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: No confidential value may be referenced through `import.meta.env`, a `VITE_` variable, HTML replacement, bundled JSON, source map, or other browser-delivered artifact.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Firebase web configuration and Stripe publishable keys may appear in the browser when intended for their public SDK roles. Stripe secret keys, webhook secrets, payment-provider restricted keys, Firebase service-account credentials, database URLs, and R2 access credentials must remain server-side.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: User-generated text must be rendered through React’s ordinary escaped text path. Any HTML, Markdown-derived HTML, rich text, SVG markup, or `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` use requires a documented need, an actively maintained allowlist sanitizer, and adversarial tests.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Direct DOM injection sinks—including `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, string-to-code execution, and unsafe template APIs—must be prohibited for untrusted data. Safe text and attribute APIs must be used unless the content is sanitized for the exact sink.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: User-controlled navigation destinations must be parsed with the URL API and validated against an explicit policy. Internal return paths should be relative or identifier-mapped; external destinations require allowed schemes and, where risk warrants, allowed hosts. `javascript:` and unintended `data:` destinations must be rejected.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Links that open an untrusted external page in a new browsing context must prevent opener control. Referrer suppression is a separate privacy decision and must not be confused with opener isolation.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Client-side public, authenticated, and administrator route guards must be treated only as presentation and navigation controls. Every protected operation and object access must remain enforceable by the backend on each request.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Authentication persistence must be selected through a threat model covering XSS exposure, shared devices, multi-tab behavior, usability, and provider SDK behavior. Tokens must never be logged, placed in URLs, analytics, traces, screenshots, or error messages.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Persistent browser storage must not contain payment credentials, administrator data, private messages, unrestricted presigned URLs, or other sensitive records unless a documented offline/persistence requirement and compensating controls justify it. Storage unavailability and eviction must not corrupt the application.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Sign-out, user switching, role removal, suspension, or account deletion must clear or invalidate user-scoped memory, query caches, persistent storage, saved service-worker responses, provider state, and pending requests before another identity can reuse them.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Third-party JavaScript must have an owner, purpose, data-flow review, version/update mechanism, failure behavior, and removal process. CSP, Trusted Types, SRI, self-hosting, npm bundling, or direct provider hosting must be selected according to how the provider distributes and updates the script.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: A Content Security Policy and Trusted Types enforcement should be evaluated and progressively deployed using reporting before enforcement. They are defense-in-depth and do not replace output encoding, sanitization, or safe DOM APIs.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Frontend telemetry must use a field-level allowlist or equivalent redaction that excludes bearer tokens, payment client secrets, presigned URLs, messages, form values, email addresses unless justified, administrator content, and provider credentials. Session replay requires separate masking and privacy approval.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Payment Element data must remain inside provider-controlled boundaries. The frontend may handle the publishable key and scoped client secret required by the integration, but must not log or persist that client secret and must never handle live secret API keys or real card data in CI.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: The product must establish a documented accessibility conformance target. WCAG 2.2 Level AA is the recommended production baseline; once adopted, every applicable Level A and AA success criterion is a requirement, not an optional checklist item.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Native semantic HTML must be preferred. Navigation, headings, landmarks, lists, tables, buttons, links, fields, and labels must expose correct names, roles, values, relationships, and reading order. ARIA must not be used to imitate semantics already supplied by native elements.
classification: REQUIRED under the adopted WCAG target

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: All functionality must be operable by keyboard without a trap; focus order must be logical and focus indicators visible. Opening a modal must move focus appropriately, contain modal tab navigation, make background content inert, and restore focus on close.
classification: REQUIRED under the adopted WCAG target

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Forms must provide persistent programmatic labels, instructions, accessible field-level errors, a discoverable form-level summary where useful, and status announcements for asynchronous validation and submission. Error identification must not depend only on color.
classification: REQUIRED under the adopted WCAG target

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Loading, payment processing, upload processing, success, notification, and failure changes that do not move focus must be programmatically announced with appropriately noninterruptive or assertive status semantics. Announcements must not repeat continuously during background refresh.
classification: REQUIRED under the adopted WCAG target

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Interfaces must remain usable with browser zoom, text resizing, narrow viewport reflow, orientation changes, on-screen keyboards, safe areas, long content, and localization expansion. Hover-only or fine-pointer-only interactions are prohibited. Fixed breakpoints are not mandated; demonstrated behavior is.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Color contrast, non-color cues, target size, focus appearance, reduced-motion preferences, image alternatives, and nontext-content treatment must meet every applicable criterion in the chosen WCAG version and level.
classification: REQUIRED under the adopted WCAG target

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Composite widgets such as tabs, menus, and dialogs must follow a documented keyboard model and state semantics consistent with native behavior or WAI-ARIA APG patterns. A component library does not remove the need for runtime verification.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Production performance must measure LCP, INP, and CLS in field data. The current authoritative “good” thresholds are LCP ≤2.5 seconds, INP ≤200 milliseconds, and CLS ≤0.1 at the 75th percentile, separately for mobile and desktop.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: CI and pre-release testing should track laboratory performance for representative routes, devices, and network conditions. Project-specific budgets for JavaScript, images, long tasks, route waterfalls, and critical requests must be derived from field baselines and product goals rather than arbitrary universal limits.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: The browser-support policy must consider Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge, relevant mobile browsers, Firebase and Stripe support, and assistive-technology combinations. Automated coverage must be supplemented by manual device and assistive-technology testing selected from usage and risk data.

section: Frontend security, privacy, accessibility, and performance requirements
text: Failure of analytics, error monitoring, optional maps, chat widgets, or other nonessential third-party services must not block core navigation, authentication, booking, messaging, or payment recovery. Service-worker/offline behavior is not required unless explicitly adopted.

Pure formatting, parsing, validation, date/time conversion, calculation, reducer, permission-display, API-mapping, and error-mapping logic must have deterministic unit tests, especially around boundary and invalid inputs.
classification: REQUIRED where such logic is material

text: React component tests must assert user-visible behavior through roles, names, labels, text, and keyboard interactions. Private state, implementation methods, CSS structure, and shallow-render internals must not be the primary contract.

Component tests must cover loading, empty, stale, error, unauthorized, disabled, retry, success, and double-submission states applicable to the component. Asynchronous assertions must wait on observable outcomes rather than arbitrary delay.

Mocks, spies, fake timers, environment changes, and shared module state must be restored between tests. Fake timers may be used only when the tested clock is under project control and must not obscure unresolved promises or browser scheduling behavior.

The API client must be tested against successful JSON, empty response, malformed JSON, non-JSON error, validation error, unauthenticated, forbidden, rate-limited, server, timeout, cancellation, and offline/network outcomes.

Backend unit/service tests must isolate pure policy and transformation logic, while API integration tests must exercise FastAPI routing, dependency wiring, serialization, validation, error contracts, and real authorization behavior.

Dependency overrides must be scoped and restored after each test or suite. Authentication may be replaced for tests of unrelated behavior, but dedicated authorization tests must exercise the real application authorization path rather than an always-allow override.

PostgreSQL-dependent behavior must be tested against PostgreSQL. SQLite may be used for narrowly scoped tests only when the team demonstrates that dialect, type, constraint, concurrency, default, and transaction differences are irrelevant to those tests.

Database tests must use a dedicated nonproduction database, deterministic factories, isolated transactions or schema/database reset, and cleanup that succeeds even after test failure. Tests must remain order-independent and safe under configured parallelism.

Authentication and authorization coverage must include anonymous, authenticated owner, different user, suspended/deleted user, administrator, removed administrator, expired/revoked token, stale role, cross-user object ID, privileged-field injection, hidden route, and direct API access.

Mocked browser tests must serve the normal frontend while intercepting API/provider traffic at the browser boundary to deterministically exercise rare, error, empty, delayed, malformed, and out-of-order conditions. Their contract-drift limitation must be documented.

Full-stack browser tests must use the built React application, real FastAPI application, real PostgreSQL test database, controlled authentication, and no production data or live provider charges. Critical workflows must validate durable server state, not only visible success messages.

Stripe testing must use a sandbox or test mode, test keys, and documented test payment methods; real card data and live charges are prohibited in automated tests. Success, decline, additional authentication, processing, refresh, duplicate confirmation, timeout, refund, and reconciliation paths require coverage appropriate to risk.

Upload tests must distinguish filename extension, declared MIME type, actual file structure, dimensions, size, authorization, signed-URL expiry, object-key mismatch, missing/deleted objects, abandoned uploads, and duplicate completion.

Concurrency tests must deterministically coordinate competing operations—using barriers, controlled transactions, provider replay, or known scheduling points—for final-slot booking, waitlist promotion, duplicate webhook/refund/credit, provisioning, concurrent administration, and payment-versus-cancellation. Random sleeps are insufficient.

Migration tests must create or restore a production-like prior schema, apply pending migrations, verify application startup and representative reads/writes, and where rollback is claimed, test the documented rollback procedure.

Test data must be synthetic or irreversibly transformed, reproducible, timezone-aware, capable of expressing relationships and financial edge cases, and free of production credentials and unnecessary personal data. Random generation must record or fix its seed on failure.

Playwright tests must use isolated browser contexts, semantic locators, web-first assertions, and condition-based waits. Arbitrary sleeps, brittle DOM/CSS selectors, and XPath should be treated as exceptions requiring documented justification.

Saved Playwright authentication state must be treated as a credential, excluded from source control and general artifacts, isolated by role and environment, rotated or recreated as needed, and never contain production sessions.

CI browser failures must retain bounded diagnostic artifacts such as trace, screenshot, console/network summary, and relevant sanitized server logs. Video should be retained selectively where it adds diagnostic value. Artifacts must be scanned or redacted for secrets.

Retries may classify and collect evidence about flaky tests, but a test that passes only on retry must remain visible and owned. Persistent flakiness must block or be quarantined under a time-bounded exception; retries must not convert recurring defects into clean status.

Statement, branch, function, requirements, and critical-workflow coverage must be reported separately. Gates must be based on historical baseline, risk, and changed-code expectations. No universal percentage is established by the authoritative sources; exclusions require review.
Every pull request must run from a clean checkout of the reviewed revision and use an explicitly supported Node, npm, Python, and package-manager version. Toolchain changes must be reviewable.

JavaScript dependencies must be installed from a committed lockfile using a frozen clean-install operation such as `npm ci`. A mismatch between `package.json` and the lockfile must fail rather than rewrite the lockfile.

Python dependency resolution must use a committed, reviewable mechanism that fixes or hashes the complete deployable dependency set. The specific package manager is context-dependent, but CI must not silently resolve unconstrained production dependencies.

Formatting verification, JavaScript/React linting, Python linting, frontend type checking, and backend type checking where adopted must run noninteractively and fail on newly introduced blocking violations. Suppressions require local justification.

Secret scanning must cover commits and pull-request diffs and should cover repository history, CI logs, bundles, source maps, test fixtures, screenshots, traces, artifacts, and container layers. A confirmed credential exposure requires revocation/rotation, not only deletion.

Pull requests that change dependency manifests or lockfiles must receive dependency review identifying added, removed, or changed transitive packages and known advisories. High-risk changes require owner review.

Static security analysis must inspect directly relevant unsafe patterns, including raw HTML sinks, dangerous URL construction, command or subprocess injection, unsafe SQL construction, workflow expression injection, and hard-coded credentials. No single analyzer is sufficient proof of safety.

Pull requests must run frontend unit/component tests, backend unit/integration tests, and all deterministic required negative security tests. Test reports and coverage artifacts must be published even on failure where safe.
Schema-changing pull requests must run migration verification against PostgreSQL. Every release candidate must verify that the deployable backend artifact and migration set are mutually compatible.

CI must create the exact production frontend build and backend package/container intended for release. A production build failure, forbidden bundle value, missing asset, or invalid container build must block release.

Required browser tests must run against a production build. The blocking pull-request subset must cover critical deterministic workflows; broader browser, device, provider, and long-running suites may run on merge, release, or schedule according to risk.

Required status checks and required reviews must protect the default and release branches. Force pushes and deletion must be disabled absent a documented emergency procedure; bypass authority must be restricted and auditable.

Deployment jobs must use protected environments or equivalent approval boundaries, with separate staging and production credentials. Untrusted pull-request jobs must never gain production secrets or deployment authority.

Release must require successful designated checks, reviewed security exceptions, migration readiness, known-failure disposition, artifact identity, and deployment approval. Post-deployment smoke tests must verify revision identity and safe critical paths; failure must stop promotion or invoke rollback procedure.

Dependency manifests and lockfiles must be committed and reviewed together. Lockfile-only changes, unexpected registry changes, new install scripts, ownership changes, and large transitive additions require scrutiny.

Dependency updates must arrive through reviewable pull requests, separate emergency security updates from routine upgrades, consult release notes for breaking changes, and run the full relevant test/build suite. Major updates and abandoned packages require explicit migration assessment.

Vulnerability management must combine ecosystem advisories, dependency review, repository alerts, Python advisory sources, container/OS scanning, and code-oriented analysis as applicable. Findings require owner, severity/exploitability assessment, remediation or accepted-risk rationale, and expiry for suppressions.

Third-party GitHub Actions or equivalent CI extensions must be pinned to an immutable full commit SHA where the platform permits. Any human-readable tag must be informational only, and update PRs must review the new commit and action changes.

Each workflow and job must declare the minimum `GITHUB_TOKEN` or equivalent permissions needed. Read-only defaults are preferred; write, package, attestation, deployment, and identity-token permissions must be granted only to the jobs that use them.

Untrusted pull-request values must not be directly interpolated into shell scripts or executable code. `pull_request_target` must not check out and execute untrusted head code with base-repository secrets; use ordinary `pull_request` for untrusted code unless a narrowly designed privileged workflow is necessary.

Cloud and deployment authentication should use OIDC or an equivalent federated, short-lived credential mechanism where supported. Long-lived keys require documented inability to federate, least privilege, rotation, environment isolation, and approval protection.

CI caches must use keys that include trusted lockfile/toolchain identity and must not permit untrusted jobs to overwrite caches later consumed by privileged jobs without validation. Cache contents must never contain secrets.

Hosted runners are preferred for untrusted pull requests unless self-hosted runners are ephemeral, isolated, and designed for hostile code. Persistent self-hosted runners must not expose internal networks, residual credentials, or previous-job state to untrusted changes.

Release artifacts must carry a source revision, build identifier, cryptographic digest, environment-independent identity, and retention metadata. Promotion should reuse the same verified artifact when configuration architecture permits rather than silently rebuilding different bits for production.

Generate an SBOM for production container images and other distributable artifacts when supported, and retain it with artifact identity. The SBOM must include the relevant final artifact and, where risk warrants, build-stage dependencies not present in the final image.

Build provenance or artifact attestations should be generated by the hosted build platform and verified before high-risk promotion. The target SLSA level must be selected according to product risk; the highest level is not automatically required.

Container build configuration must be validated and the final image must be built in CI. Build warnings, unpinned or mutable base-image policy, secret use in build arguments, and attestation disclosure must be addressed according to documented policy.
classification: REQUIRED if containers are release artifacts

text: Document the production topology, trust boundaries, public entry points, private services, inbound ports, outbound provider dependencies, regions and single points of failure.
Host the static frontend, API, workers and scheduler as independently deployable responsibilities; a scheduler must have singleton or duplicate-safe semantics.
Keep API instances stateless with respect to authoritative sessions, rate limits, jobs, locks, uploads and user data; state needed across requests or instances must use a shared durable system.
Validate all required configuration at startup and fail readiness—not silently default—when production-critical values are absent, malformed, cross-environment or unsafe.

Provide distinct startup, liveness and readiness semantics where supported. Readiness must remove an instance from traffic; it must not fail merely because a noncritical external provider is transiently unavailable.

On termination, stop accepting traffic, allow a documented grace period for in-flight requests and leased jobs, release leases safely, close database/provider clients, and terminate forcibly only after the grace period.
Configure restart policy and alerts so crashes recover but persistent startup failures produce a visible restart-loop incident rather than unlimited silent cycling.
Design rolling releases so old and new frontend, API, worker, webhook and job consumers can overlap; schema changes must use a compatibility sequence or explicitly stop incompatible workloads.
Every release must have a predeclared rollback or roll-forward decision, including treatment of irreversible migrations, emitted job formats, cached assets, provider settings and user-visible state.
Promote the same immutable release artifact across environments; identify container and frontend releases by immutable digest/version, with retained prior artifacts sufficient for rollback.

Terminate public traffic with HTTPS, use supported TLS, automate renewal, monitor certificate failure/expiry, align frontend/API domains and redirects, and remove dangling DNS when a service is retired.

Measure capacity against API concurrency, DB connections, worker throughput, storage, provider quotas, log cardinality and peak operations; configure resource and budget alerts before known limits are reached.
Use a multi-stage build or equivalent so compilers, Node build tools, test dependencies, package caches and other build-only material are absent from the runtime image.
Use a trusted, maintained base; pin an intentional version and record the resolved digest. Rebuild and rescan when the base or dependencies receive security updates.

Do not pass secrets through Dockerfile `ARG`, persistent `ENV`, copied files, labels, image layers, cache, or build logs. Use supported ephemeral build-secret mounts only when a build step truly needs a secret.
Run the application as a dedicated non-root UID/GID, with only required file ownership and no dependence on writing privileged paths.
classification: REQUIRED unless the platform provides a documented equivalent isolation boundary

text: Prohibit privileged mode, Docker socket mounts, host PID/network namespaces and unnecessary host-filesystem mounts; drop unneeded Linux capabilities and retain a seccomp/AppArmor/SELinux policy where supported.
Use a read-only root filesystem where supported, with explicit bounded writable locations for temporary or runtime files; never use local container storage as authoritative persistence.
Set CPU, memory and process limits appropriate to measured workload; monitor throttling, out-of-memory termination and crash loops.
Use executable-form entrypoint/command and ensure the application process receives signals directly or through a signal-aware init; do not use development reload mode in production.

Exclude `.env` files, service-account files, repository metadata not needed at runtime, tests, local data, package caches, coverage output and developer artifacts through build context controls such as `.dockerignore`.

Scan images and dependencies before release and continuously for newly disclosed vulnerabilities; sign or attest images when the registry/platform and threat model can operationally enforce verification.
Store production secrets in a managed secret store or hosting-platform secret facility with access control and auditability; inject them only at runtime.

Treat environment variables as an acceptable compatibility mechanism only when the platform protects them and no safer file/identity method exists; document exposure through process metadata, dumps, support tools and child processes.
Scope each database, Firebase, Stripe, R2, CI, hosting, DNS, monitoring, encryption and backup credential to one environment and the minimum operations required.
Prefer attached workload identity, managed identity or OIDC/workload-identity federation for Google/Firebase and CI-to-cloud access where supported; avoid downloadable service-account keys.
classification: STRONGLY RECOMMENDED; REQUIRED where organizational policy prohibits keys

text: Where Stripe, R2 or another provider requires a long-lived secret, use a restricted key/token when available, store it centrally, prevent client exposure and maintain a tested replacement path.

Maintain planned and emergency rotation procedures for every secret category, including dependency owners, overlap support, deployment/restart impact, validation, revocation and audit evidence. Do not invent a universal interval.

Redact secrets from application logs, CI output, crash reports, traces, error-monitoring breadcrumbs, support tickets, administrative dashboards and exports; detection of a leaked token must initiate incident response.
Human production access must use named accounts, provider-supported MFA, least-privilege roles and periodic review; shared day-to-day accounts are prohibited.

Offboarding must remove repository, deployment, hosting, DB, Firebase, Stripe, Cloudflare, DNS, monitoring, backup and secret access, revoke sessions/tokens where supported, and transfer ownership or recovery methods.

Maintain separately protected provider-owner and domain-recovery paths. Break-glass use must be logged, alerted, limited to an emergency, reviewed afterward and followed by rotation where exposure is possible.
Emit structured records with UTC timestamp, severity, service, environment, release, event name, request/job correlation, safe route template, status/outcome and duration where applicable.

Sanitize control characters and untrusted log fields, bound message size, and never record raw credentials, auth tokens, private-message content, card data, secret keys, database connection strings or unnecessary personal data.
Collect container stdout/stderr and material edge, database, provider, deployment and job events centrally; protect access, encryption, export and deletion according to data classification.
Define a documented retention and deletion policy for each telemetry class based on diagnostic, security, privacy, legal-review and cost needs. Do not retain “forever” by default.
Measure API request volume, successful outcome/error rate, latency distributions, in-flight work, timeouts and status categories using route templates rather than raw paths.

Measure PostgreSQL connection and pool usage, query latency, slow queries, locks/deadlocks, storage, replication if used, and maintenance/autovacuum health; alert before exhaustion becomes user impact.
Measure worker pending count, oldest pending age, processing latency, attempts, failures, dead letters, active workers and expired leases; distinguish retryable from permanent failure.

Monitor payment attempts and terminal outcomes, webhook delivery and processing failures, refund failures, disputes where applicable, unknown outcomes, and reconciliation mismatches against Stripe records.
Monitor upload attempts/failures, validation/processing failures, object deletion failures, storage usage and orphan/reference mismatches; separate irreplaceable originals from derived assets.

Do not use user IDs, emails, request IDs, provider event IDs, object keys, raw URLs or other unbounded values as metric labels. Use bounded categories and place detailed identifiers in protected logs or traces.

Adopt distributed tracing when cross-service or asynchronous diagnosis justifies its cost; propagate standard trace context across API, provider calls and jobs, but do not propagate secrets or unnecessary identity in baggage.
Configure frontend, backend and worker error monitoring by release and environment; protect source maps, request context, breadcrumbs and session replay with explicit privacy review and sampling.
Maintain dashboards for API, database, workers, payments/webhooks/refunds, storage, authentication, moderation/admin failures, deployments, capacity, backups, provider status and cost.

Alerts must be actionable, routed to an owner, deduplicated, suppressible during approved maintenance, tested end-to-end, and based primarily on user/business symptoms; cause alerts should aid diagnosis.
Derive alert thresholds from baseline behavior, user impact, backlog recovery rate, provider limits, selected SLOs and response time; document the rationale and review false positives/negatives.

Define internal SLIs for critical journeys—such as listing games, booking, payment processing, webhook processing and worker delay—and approve practical objectives; a public SLA and formal error-budget freeze policy are context-dependent.

Use external synthetic checks for DNS, TLS, homepage and basic API availability. Authenticated booking, upload or administrative transactions require isolated test accounts, safe test mode and cleanup and are context-dependent.
classification: Basic checks: REQUIRED; complex transactions: CONTEXT-DEPENDENT

text: Subscribe to and correlate Firebase, Stripe, Cloudflare, database, hosting and DNS provider incident notifications, but verify internal symptoms before attributing an incident solely to a provider.
Maintain a concise incident-response plan defining incident criteria, severity, declaration authority, incident lead, technical lead, communications, evidence handling, escalation and closure.

Establish reachable escalation for application, database, financial, provider-account, DNS/domain and privacy incidents. A staffed 24-hour on-call rotation is context-dependent on commitments and risk.
Record a factual incident timeline, decisions, commands or configuration changes, affected releases/accounts/resources and preserved relevant logs without copying secrets unnecessarily.

Secret-exposure runbooks must include immediate disable/revocation where safe, replacement, deployment dependency handling, access/session review, log search, scope determination, provider coordination and validation.

Financial incidents must stop further duplicate or unsafe processing, preserve Stripe and internal event identifiers, determine all affected users/transactions, reconcile, repair through an approved process, and retain an audit trail.
Define for each provider outage which functions fail closed, degrade, queue, retry or remain available; do not make the entire site unavailable solely because a noncritical dependency is down.

Maintain runbooks for API/DB outage, DB connection exhaustion, failed deployment/migration, worker backlog/dead letters, Stripe webhook and reconciliation failure, R2 failure/compromise, Firebase outage, admin compromise, certificate expiry, backup failure/restore, and deletion failure.

Every runbook must include trigger, impact check, prerequisites, safe diagnostic steps, containment, decision authority, rollback/recovery, validation, communications, escalation and evidence to retain.
Conduct blameless post-incident review for material incidents, tracking causes, contributing controls, user/business impact, detection gaps, action owners, priority and completion evidence.

Use lightweight but recorded change management: peer review, migration/config/provider-change review, owner, validation, rollback or roll-forward plan and post-deployment check. Emergency changes require retrospective review.
Monitor operating cost and abuse signals across hosting, DB, R2 operations/storage, Stripe fees, Firebase, logs, metrics, CI and backups; route material anomalies to technical and financial owners.
Test incident communication channels and alert delivery independently of the primary application and normal identity path.
Complete a business-impact assessment and approve RPO and RTO separately for PostgreSQL, R2 originals, payments/reconciliation, audit records, messages, configuration, secrets and jobs.

Enable automated PostgreSQL backups with encryption, restricted backup access, monitored completion and a documented retention decision; protect backup credentials separately from normal application credentials.
Enable PITR when the approved database RPO cannot be met by periodic snapshots or logical backups; verify the actual WAL retention window and recovery controls in the provider.
classification: CONTEXT-DEPENDENT, becoming REQUIRED when selected RPO requires it

text: Ensure the recovery set covers database contents plus required roles, ownership, extensions, configuration and version compatibility. A provider snapshot alone is insufficient unless restore testing proves complete recovery.

Treat backup-job success as input, not proof. Restore PostgreSQL into an isolated environment and validate decryption, selected point, row/relation integrity, application startup, Firebase identity mapping, Stripe reconciliation references, R2 references and job state.
Select restore-test frequency from change rate, business impact, backup technology and team capacity; execute after material backup, database-version, extension or encryption-key changes.

Classify R2 objects as replaceable derivatives or irreplaceable originals. For irreplaceable objects, implement recovery protection sufficient for the approved RPO, such as bucket locks where appropriate and an independent copy or source-of-truth strategy.
classification: REQUIRED decision; recovery copy REQUIRED when loss tolerance demands it

text: Do not assume unsupported R2 versioning, replication or selective backup deletion. Record the exact current account capabilities and chosen object-recovery design.

Maintain recoverable records of hosting configuration, DNS, TLS, Firebase settings, Stripe webhooks/API versions, R2 settings, DB settings, IAM, monitoring, alerts, schedules and secret references through infrastructure as code or controlled configuration documentation.

Document recovery from lost MFA devices, recovery codes, provider owner accounts, registrar access, secret-manager access and backup credentials. Test the workflow without disclosing production secret values.

Maintain a compromise-resistant recovery path: isolated or immutable copies where feasible, independent credentials, clean rebuild procedures, and validation that compromised identities or artifacts are not restored.

Define recovery sequencing for regional/provider failure: establish control-plane access, DNS/edge, database, secrets/configuration, API/workers, object references, payment reconciliation and user communication.
Preserve durable deletion/anonymization tombstones or an equivalent replayable record so restoration of an older backup does not silently reactivate data previously deleted from active systems.
classification: STRONGLY RECOMMENDED; REQUIRED where restore can reintroduce personal data

text: Exercise database restore, failed deployment, credential compromise, provider outage, R2 deletion, DNS recovery and financial reconciliation at a risk-based cadence, with owners and tracked corrective actions.
classification: REQUIRED exercise program; individual frequency CONTEXT-DEPENDENT

text: Maintain an approved classification covering public, internal, confidential and highly sensitive data, including identity data, private messages, financial metadata, moderation evidence, audit records, logs, images, provider IDs and secrets.

Collect and derive only data needed for a documented product, security, financial or operational purpose; review optional profile fields, IP/user-agent storage, provider payload copies, administrative notes, analytics, replay and debug data.

Approve a retention schedule for every requested category—accounts, profiles, games, bookings, waitlists, messages, notices, payments/refunds/credits, Stripe identifiers, images, moderation, administrative records, logs, metrics, backups, exports and test data.
Do not invent durations. Document for each duration the operational purpose, financial integrity, security need, user expectation, privacy impact, legal-review input, backup behavior and cost.

Implement account deletion as a durable, retryable workflow covering Firebase identity, local account/profile, participation and hosted content, messages, notifications, images, provider references, pending jobs and applicable anonymization or restricted retention.

For each record type, decide among hard deletion, anonymization/de-identification, soft deletion or restricted retention. Soft-deleted data must not remain generally visible or indefinitely retained without purpose.

Document that deleted data may remain in immutable or rotating backups until expiry; prevent ordinary use of those copies, and reapply deletion/anonymization after restore. Do not claim selective deletion unless the backup product supports and verifies it.

Provide authenticated operational procedures for data access, correction, export and deletion requests, including identity verification, authorization, secure format/delivery, expiration, download logging, retries and prevention of cross-user data inclusion.
classification: REQUIRED capability where such operations are offered or required by policy

text: Administrative exports must be least-privilege, approved where risk warrants, encrypted in transit and at rest, time-limited, access-logged and automatically deleted according to policy.

Production data must not be copied into development or test by default. Use synthetic data; any approved staging copy must be minimized, de-identified, separately authorized, protected and deleted on a documented schedule.
Separate technical health metrics from business analytics and restrict user-level analytics identifiers and session replay under explicit purpose, access, retention and consent review.

A privacy incident involving exports, logs, staging data, messages, images or credentials must use the incident process, preserve scope evidence, contain access and support jurisdiction-specific notification review without assuming a legal conclusion.

Firebase production must use an identified production project separated from development/test; verify enabled providers, authorized domains, Identity Platform/MFA decision, service accounts and keys, IAM, audit availability, templates, quotas, billing and recovery owners.
Verify Firebase API-key restrictions but do not treat Firebase client API keys as authentication secrets; protect actual administrative credentials and project IAM.

Stripe production must verify live/test separation, API version, webhook endpoints and event versions, required event selection, failed delivery monitoring, restricted keys, team roles, enforced MFA, recovery owners, disputes/payout alerts as applicable, and reconciliation access.
Stripe webhook recovery must support review and controlled replay of undelivered events with idempotent operational handling; automatic provider retry must not be the only recovery plan.

R2 production must verify bucket identity, private/public status, custom domain, `r2.dev` status, token scopes, CORS, lifecycle rules, locks, deletion controls, usage/billing and environment separation.

Verify managed PostgreSQL version/support status, TLS, private networking or tightly restricted ingress, database users, superuser access, connection limits, storage, backups/PITR, maintenance, upgrades, monitoring, deletion protection and recovery contacts.

Protect registrar and DNS access with named accounts and MFA; inventory apex, `www`, API, staging, preview, webhook and R2 records; automate TLS renewal and monitor domain/certificate expiration and dangling records.
Decide whether to enable DNSSEC based on registrar/provider support, operational competence and recovery/migration procedure; if enabled, monitor DS state and test nameserver-change procedures.
Use CAA where supported to constrain certificate authorities and document HSTS scope, preload decision and subdomain implications; neither setting substitutes for certificate monitoring and renewal.

Repository and deployment access must use named roles, protected production environments, reviewed changes and short-lived OIDC/workload credentials where the platform supports them; avoid shared deploy tokens.

Subscribe named owners to provider security, outage, billing, quota, key/certificate expiration, failed backup, dispute and payout notifications relevant to enabled services; test that messages reach a monitored channel.
Record safe evidence of provider settings without secrets: resource IDs, role names, scopes, modes, versions, dates and redacted screenshots/exports. Review dashboard drift after material change.
